"In recent months Russia has increased in attempts to conduct sabotage against European defence related facilities," the statement said.

"This activity is typically characterised by the use of proxy actors employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson," it continued, adding that such activity was intended to "undermine support" for Kyiv.

The alert warned that any organisations involved in military procurement or supplying equipment to Ukraine could be a target.

It also offered a number of steps on how companies could reduce their exposure to "hostile reconnaissance," detect and report suspicious activity and minimise the impact of any attacks.

In a separate statement, Westminster announced that closed-door security briefings were also to be given to defence sector and critical national infrastructure CEOs on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"Both the briefings and the alert will set out actions organisations can take to protect their sites, people and operations amidst the changing threat landscape," it said.

The warnings follow a fresh wave of security incidents across Europe in recent weeks, including airspace violations and reported cyber and sabotage attacks.

UK Security Minister Dan Jarvis said that recent sabotage attempts across the continent demonstrated the "seriousness of the threats we face."

"It’s truly shameful that actors are seeking to disrupt our way of life and that of our allies, especially targeting organisations doing vital work in support of Ukraine," he added.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has repeatedly signalled his support for Ukraine as it continues to fight against Russia's ongoing invasion.

The letter signed by 76 MEPs targets a controversial plan to set up a centre in Rwanda for migrants with no legal right to stay in Europe.

A total of seventy-six MEPs have challenged the legality of plans by five EU countries to deport irregular migrants to Rwanda from 2027, and are asking the European Commission for an assessment of the country's human rights record.

In a letter seen by Euronews and sent on Tuesday to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner, the MEPs warned that Rwanda may not meet the human rights standards required under EU law for return hubs outside the bloc.

“Besides general human rights concerns, Rwanda has a particular reputation for serious maltreatment of refugees and asylum seekers in the recent past,” the letter says, challenging the initiative launched by Austria, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands and Denmark.

Most of the signatories come from centre-left and left-wing political groups, which have consistently opposed the EU legislation paving the way for the creation of return hubs.

They fear that Rwanda is “unable to fulfil the conditions” required to host a return hub, namely compliance with international human rights standards and international law.

Under the law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc, only non-EU countries “where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected” are eligible.

The MEPs consider this unlikely to be the case in Rwanda, although the final details of the deal are still under negotiation.

“The Rwandan government under President Paul Kagame is notorious for its harassment, espionage, detention and transnational repression of dissidents and political opposition,” reads the letter.

The lawmakers also condemned Rwanda’s involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which has led to “violations of international law and the displacement of millions of persons”.

The European Parliament has previously adopted a firm stance towards Rwanda.

In February 2025, it called for the suspension of an EU-Rwanda memorandum of understanding on critical raw materials, citing alleged war crimes and the occupation of Congolese territory by Rwanda’s defence forces.

Under EU law, the European Commission can initiate an assessment of Rwanda's human rights record, but it has no formal role in approving the plan.

The deportations, expected to begin in 2027, could nonetheless face legal challenges before European courts.

Ukraine's naval drone strikes on two Russian vessels in and off Benghazi have alarmed Italy, amid fears that the attacks could reignite Libya's civil war.

Kyiv has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russian ships in the Mediterranean Sea, but Italy fears the strikes could escalate into renewed fighting in Libya, destabilising its southern neighbour in one of Rome's worst nightmares.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani voiced his concern over Ukraine's operations in Libya to his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday, according to a readout of the phone call.

On Sunday, Ukrainian naval drones hit two Russian vessels, one docked at the Benghazi naval base and the other just off the Libyan city. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it an "exemplary Ukrainian operation."

The attacks appear to be part of a broader maritime campaign against Russian vessels beyond the Black Sea. On Saturday, a Ukrainian drone hit another Russian ship near Finland's territorial waters.

But the strikes in Libya have rung alarm bells in Rome, where even the prospect of civil war reopening across the Mediterranean is enough to send a shiver down officials' spines.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has so far refrained from commenting on the episode publicly to avoid escalating the situation, but according to the Italian daily la Repubblica, she privately slammed the attacks as "unacceptable".

"We were not informed of absolutely anything; we did not provide any kind of support to the Ukrainians, they did everything without informing us," Tajani told reporters on the sidelines of a visit to Baku.

Tajani pledged to work to stop the conflict with Russia spreading across the Mediterranean basin, while respecting Libya's sovereignty and avoiding its destabilisation.

Libya has been split since the civil war that followed the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. A UN-recognised government in Tripoli controls much of the west, while the east is dominated by military strongman Khalifa Haftar and his Libyan National Army, which is backed by the rival administration in Benghazi.

Russia backs Haftar, while Italy supports the Tripoli government. Turkey has also been increasing its military presence in the region since it intervened in 2019 to stop Haftar capturing Tripoli.

For Rome, a renewed explosion of fighting in Libya, sparked by possible Russian retaliation in the country, is a nightmare scenario that evokes the chaos following Gaddafi's death.

Italy can do little but hope the strikes do not trigger renewed fighting between Libya's rival factions. Domestically, the Italian government also sees the risk that the attacks might undermine political support for the aid to Ukraine.

"We all know that Libya and the Mediterranean Sea have been a zone of Russian intervention for a long time. Italian politics prefers to ignore international developments rather than taking responsibility to try to prevent an escalation," MEP Lucia Annunziata (Italy/S&D) told Euronews.

Annunziata argued that Kyiv should have notified Rome of the attacks, but stressed that the Italian government cannot simultaneously recognise Ukraine's right to self-defence while imposing geographical limits on how it exercises that right.

Italy is not alone in its concern over the new flurry of Ukrainian attacks on Russian vessels. On Tuesday, a German government spokesperson warned against escalation in the Baltic Sea region.

In May, Greek fishermen found an unexploded Ukrainian naval drone in the Ionian Sea, prompting a strong reaction from Athens, which wants to keep the Mediterranean from becoming a theatre of military operations.

"Ukraine's right to self-defence cannot justify such actions," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lana Zochiou said when Athens lodged a formal protest in June.

According to an EU official who spoke with Euronews on condition of anonymity, Ukraine intended to send a clear signal that Russian vessels in the Mediterranean are within arm's reach, forcing them to reroute and raising the costs for Moscow.

"No member state wants to see the war in its backyard," the official said. "But the spillover didn't start two days ago. Russia is violating EU territory every day of the week. Russian vessels are a legitimate military target."

Înmatriculările de autoturisme noi în Uniunea Europeană au crescut cu +5,4% între ianuarie și octombrie, ajungând la 9,46 milioane de vehicule, anunță Asociația Producătorilor Europeni de Automobile (ACEA).

Înmatriculările de autoturisme complet electrice, alimentate exclusiv de baterii, au crescut cu +56,1%, iar cele ale vehiculelor hibride plug-in au avansat cu +9,2%. În schimb, înmatriculările autoturismelor hibride clasice au scăzut ușor, cu -0,3% în octombrie 2026, față de aceeași lună a anului trecut.

Autoturismele hibrid non-plug-in reprezintă în continuare cea mai mare pondere din vânzări (36%, sau 3,4 milioane de mașini). Cu toate acestea, piața își continuă tendința de electrificare, acest tip de sistem de propulsie reprezentând acum 23,4% din înmatriculări (față de 16,4% în octombrie 2025), sau 2,21 milioane de vehicule.

Mașinile pe benzină, pe de altă parte, își continuă declinul, cota lor de piață reducându-se de la 27,4% la 20,8%. De asemenea, și înmatriculările de motoare diesel (6,9% din vânzări) au scăzut cu -20,6%.

Vehiculele electrice (hibride plug-in și non-plug-in, precum și vehicule electrice) au reprezentat aproape 70% din piața europeană în octombrie. În primele zece luni ale anului, vânzările de mașini electrice au crescut cu +50%, impulsionate de anumite piețe: Franța (+79,4%), Germania (+60,7%) și Danemarca (+41%). Piața auto franceză, acum a doua cea mai mare din UE după Germania, a crescut cu +4,4% în primele zece luni ale anului.

În privința producătorilor, ofensiva chineză continuă. BYD, cel mai mare grup chinez de pe piața europeană, a înregistrat o creștere a înmatriculărilor cu +118% în primele zece luni ale anului 2026, chiar dacă vânzările sale reprezintă doar 237.137 de vehicule de la începutul anului, din peste 9 milioane de înmatriculări noi. Vânzările Chery Automobile au crescut cu +150% (159.278 de vehicule din ianuarie), iar XPeng cu +165%.

În paralel, companiile europene Volkswagen, Renault și Stellantis au continuat să piardă teren, înregistrările autovehiculelor lor scăzând cu -7,6%, -9,8% și, respectiv, -8% față de aceeași perioadă a anului trecut⁠.

Italy's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told Euronews that Rome has sought to expand its business relations with Baku now that peace has brought stability and improved connectivity to the region.

Italy has sought to invest in the emerging Middle Corridor transit route connecting Asia to Europe through the South Caucasus and boost its business volumes with its "strategic partner" Azerbaijan, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told Euronews in Baku on Monday.

With Italy as the top EU importer of energy from Azerbaijan and one of its largest commercial partners, Tajani and Azerbaijan's Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov led an Azerbaijan-Italy Business Forum that brought together business leaders from both countries, with the two countries sharing a "strong relationship built on trust and common interests."

During a Euronews interview at the forum, the Italian foreign minister, who is also deputy prime minister, told Euronews that "we must be ambitious," describing the forum's objective as "a leap in quality" and calling for a stronger economic partnership between Italy and Azerbaijan.

"Azerbaijan is at the heart of a region that is increasingly important to our foreign policy," Tajani said in a statement, adding that he "reaffirmed Italy’s full support for the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia, which is essential to the region’s stability and growth."

Tajani announced that Italian exports to Azerbaijan increased by 14% in the first 8 months of this year.

Tajani described Italy's strong interest in Azerbaijan’s role in the Middle Corridor transit project, saying Italian companies can bring their engineering expertise and technology, together with AI, machinery, agri-food and railways.

"We devoted considerable attention to connectivity and the diversification of energy and logistics corridors: from the Middle Corridor to the Green Energy Corridor, which could bring energy to Europe and is already attracting strong interest from our Italian companies," Tajani said.

"We are working together in a spirit of friendship towards a common goal: strengthening links between Europe and Asia and creating new opportunities for growth for our countries," the Italian foreign minister added.

The Middle Corridor is an emerging strategic transit and trade route between Asia and Europe and a strong Eurasian alternative amid global supply chain disruptions in the Middle East.

EU countries are actively exploring new investment opportunities along the Middle Corridor, a rail and maritime transport network that will connect China, Southeast Asia, and Central Asia to European markets via the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus, then to the Black Sea and onward to the Mediterranean.

Tajani also met with Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev and shared on X that he was on a “mission” to Azerbaijan, describing the country as “a strategic partner of Italy with which we share a strong relationship built on trust and common interests.”

Italian and Azerbaijani officials and business delegations discussed investments and cooperation in manufacturing, infrastructure, transport, technology, and critical raw materials.

Tajani said the two countries should work together on critical raw materials, including in Africa and other parts of the world, after signing a Joint Declaration on Strategic Cooperation in Critical Raw Materials in Rome in October.

"If you want to compete at a global level", Tajani told Euronews, "you need to reduce the price of raw materials for example."

"It's also possible to invest in Italy for companies coming from Azerbaijan, but also for Italian companies to export to Azerbaijan", he said. 

Tajani also reflected on the role peace might play in the future of business, saying "peace is a good choice for paving the way for new investments."

"I want to thank Azerbaijan for its engagement in favour of peace, not only with Armenia but also in this part of the world, during the difficult situation", he said.

"We need countries working for peace," the Italian foreign minister added.

Economic diversification and development

Azerbaijan’s Jabbarov told Euronews that the two countries signed several agreements during the forum covering AI, industrial production, construction, public transport and investment cooperation.

As both countries aim to increase Azerbaijan's gas supplies to Italy, Jabbarov said economic diversification and business developments in the non-oil sector were also a focus of the talks, including industrial parks and free economic zones, adding that “cooperation with Italian companies opens up very good opportunities for our companies.”

Jabbarov told Euronews that Azerbaijan wanted to improve the competitiveness of locally produced goods and increase their access to foreign markets.

"The initiatives are aimed at modernising industrial enterprises, expanding production capacity, facilitating access to international markets for industrial products, accelerating the adoption of digital technologies and strengthening business and investment ties," Azerbaijan's minister of economy said.

Italy’s Leonardo, a major aerospace, defence and security company, and Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Economy signed a memorandum on cooperation in high-performance computing systems and artificial intelligence.

Italy’s development finance institution, Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP), signed an agreement with Azerbaijan’s Business Development Fund, and its Head of International Markets Development Laurent Franciosi described the platform as being "capable of connecting the different dimensions of the bilateral economic relationship between the two countries.”

Speaking about the agreement with Azerbaijan’s Business Development Fund, Franciosi said: “We don’t want it to be just an institutional framework.”

**Role of small and medium-sized businesses **

Vice President of Confindustria’s Small Industry section Fausto Mazzali led the talks on cooperation among smaller businesses, telling Euronews that “for the Italian industry, Azerbaijan does not just want to be a market for development, but a country with which to build new investment opportunities and collaboration.”

Mazzali highlighted potential cooperation in infrastructure, transport and logistics, critical materials, metallurgy, automation, robotics, electronics, pharmaceuticals, and agricultural machinery, and said Italian companies could contribute through exports, but also by sharing technology, expertise, and industrial solutions.

Head of Foreign Relations at the Italian Union of Chambers of Commerce Pietro Infante said that he would like to propose "a change of paradigm,” calling for businesses to move “beyond the traditional commercial partnerships” and the “logics of pure import and export”, towards joint ventures, industrial partnerships and technology development.

Società Italiana per le Imprese all'Estero (SIMEST), majority-owned by CDP, also discussed support for Italian companies seeking to expand abroad.

Its Chief External Relations Officer Francesca Alicata outlined the institution’s role in helping businesses enter new markets, saying their mission was to support the companies, and in particular, " small and medium-sized companies.”

Alicata explained that SIMEST provided financial instruments to support international expansion, including financing, grants and support for joint ventures.

She also described supplier credit, which allows Italian companies to offer overseas customers extended payment terms for machinery and industrial equipment.

SIMEST signed an agreement with the Italy-Azerbaijan Chamber of Commerce and the Small and Medium Business Development Agency of Azerbaijan; Italy’s Investment and Export Promotion Agency and the Italian Trade Agency signed a memorandum to support trade and investment links.

Attracting investment into Italy was another subject covered at the forum.

Augusto Reggiani, Director of the Foreign Investments Attraction Unit at Italy’s Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy, explained the support available to international investors.

Meanwhile, Baku Steel Company signed an agreement with Italian companies Dismas Trading and Edgar H. Greenham to promote exports of locally manufactured industrial products.

The Azerbaijan Construction Products Manufacturers Association and Italy’s FINCO agreed to develop cooperation in construction and building materials.

Iveco and AZ Tex Import signed an agreement in the public transport sector.

Another contract, between North West Construction and Italy’s Falorni Tech, concerned the modernisation of the Garadagh Glass Plant.

The business forum follows Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni's talks with President Aliyev in May, focusing on expanding Azerbaijan's oil and gas supplies to Italy, which Meloni said had been "decisive for the energy security" of Italy since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.

At the time, Meloni said she wanted Italy to serve as Azerbaijan's "privileged gateway to the European market" as a hub between Europe and Asia.

Bilateral trade reached €10.2 billion last year, making Italy Azerbaijan's largest commercial partner, while Azerbaijan has invested around €3 billion in Italy.

Two lung drugs and more in the works

Brinsupri treats bronchiectasis, a long-term condition in which the airways widen and clog with mucus. Arikayce is used to treat adults with mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), which is a bacterial lung infection.

Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic are urging Brussels to rethink the EU's carbon pricing scheme for buildings and road transport, warning that soaring energy prices make its planned 2028 launch untenable.

In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on November 23, seen by Euronews, the Visegrad Group leaders warn that the Emissions Trading System (ETS2) could cost households and businesses tens of billions of euros, hitting consumption, employment and investment.

“According to verifiable calculations, the Emission Trading Scheme 2 (ETS2) is set to impose an additional gross burden of tens of billions of euros from 2028 onwards,” reads the letter sent to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 23 November.

“If we do not address this issue in a timely and effective manner, there is a risk of a decline in household consumption (…) and a subsequent spillover effect on corporate revenues, employment and investment.”

EU leaders asked the Commission at their 15–16 October summit to update its assessment of ETS2. The four governments are stepping up pressure ahead of another summit on 26–27 November aimed at securing a deal on the EU's long-term budget.

Unlike the existing ETS, which covers power generation and energy-intensive industries, the new system will put a carbon price on fuels used in buildings and road transport, potentially driving up heating bills and prices at the pump.

The ETS2 has already been delayed until 2028. The four governments want the first auction of emissions allowances, scheduled for January 2027, postponed until the system's future is clarified.

"This first auction should be postponed in a way that ensures legal certainty," reads the letter.

By contrast, eight other EU countries urged the Commission on 23 November to keep the expanded carbon market on track, arguing that it is crucial to accelerating electrification and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels.

The clash threatens to reopen one of the EU's most contentious climate policies, exposing deep divisions over who should bear the cost of the green transition and how to avoid a backlash from voters and businesses.

The Visegrad leaders are also putting the spotlight on who bears the cost of the EU's green transition, with governments questioning whether the EU can maintain its emissions targets without triggering a backlash from voters and businesses. Upcoming elections in France, Italy and Germany will be a key indicator.

The challenge risks reopening one of the EU's most contentious climate policies just as Brussels tries to defend its post-2030 emissions agenda.

Challenging Brussels' economic assumptions

The four governments argue that the Commission's 2021 impact assessment no longer reflects economic conditions, particularly since the US-Israeli war against Iran disrupted global energy markets.

They want Brussels to reassess the scheme using updated energy prices, inflation forecasts and carbon price scenarios, examining the impact on household purchasing power, economic growth and businesses.

They argue that a uniform carbon price could have widely differing consequences across member states, depending on household incomes, heating systems, transport alternatives and national taxation.

According to Czech research cited in the letter, the poorest 10% of households could spend 1.58% of their income on ETS2-related costs, compared with 0.5% for the wealthiest 10%.

The leaders also question whether the Social Climate Fund, designed to help vulnerable households and micro-enterprises cope with higher fuel and heating costs, will provide sufficient and timely compensation.

South Korea has repeatedly scrambled fighter jets in response to Russian military flights. Tuesday’s approach to an inhabited island brought a rare shelter warning for civilians, although the aircraft stayed outside the country’s territorial airspace.

South Korea scrambled fighter jets and told residents of an eastern island to take shelter on Tuesday after Russian air force aircraft came close to entering its territorial airspace, the military said.

The aircraft entered the Korea Air Defence Identification Zone and approached Ulleungdo island before turning away. The Joint Chiefs of Staff said no violation of South Korean territorial airspace occurred.

An air defence identification zone extends beyond national airspace and is used to identify approaching aircraft. Entering it does not by itself mean crossing into a country’s territorial airspace.

“Airspace intrusion was anticipated, therefore in order to protect the safety of our people, we issued a warning preemptively,” Jang Do-young, a spokesperson for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told a briefing on Tuesday.

The interior ministry issued the shelter warning at around 7:52 am local time (11:52 pm CET Monday), telling residents to move underground or inside buildings. It was lifted within minutes.

Conflicting messages added to the confusion. The initial alert said Russian aircraft had entered South Korean airspace. A later message from North Gyeongsang provincial authorities misidentified the aircraft as possibly North Korean. The military clarified that they were Russian and had remained outside territorial airspace.

South Korean news agency Yonhap reported that the aircraft spent about 20 minutes inside the identification zone. It said this was the first time South Korea’s military had issued a precautionary civilian alert over a possible airspace violation by Russian warplanes.

South Korea’s defence ministry summoned Russia’s military attaché Colonel Nikolai Marchenko later on Tuesday to protest and demand measures to prevent a repeat.

The ministry said repeated unannounced entries into the identification zone and the latest close approach could unnecessarily raise tensions on the Korean Peninsula and across the region.

The foreign ministry also conveyed its objections to Moscow through diplomatic channels, Yonhap reported.

Separate incidents in Poland and Japan

Poland also reported a brief Russian drone incursion late on Monday. Polish officials said the aircraft turned east and that forces had decided against shooting it down because of the potential risk to civilians.

That followed an incident on Friday in which three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland, according to Polish prosecutors.

NATO has authorised the deployment of an airborne early-warning aircraft to Poland in response to the missile incident, an alliance spokesperson confirmed on Monday. The aircraft uses radar to detect and track activity over a wide area.

Japan separately scrambled fighter jets last Thursday after two aircraft believed to be Russian briefly entered its territorial airspace near Okinoshima, off Fukuoka. Tokyo lodged a diplomatic protest with Moscow.

Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang would not return. Six days later, the chipmaker announced his reinstatement after Donald Trump pressed for his return and Elon Musk backed the campaign. Here's how the reversal unfolded and what was at stake for the AI industry.

Pressure from Silicon Valley and US President Donald Trump helped persuade Nvidia’s board to bring back Jensen Huang, 11 days after the company announced his resignation.

The US President said in a social media post, "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security". He also congratulated the board after the decision. "I made the deal," he told CNBC.

Nvidia said its board received input from senior US officials and concluded that Huang's return posed no national security risk.

The board's decision contrasts sharply with what it communicated just five days earlier. On 17 November, Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said at the start of the company’s quarterly earnings call that the board had “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”. Nvidia announced Huang's reinstatement on Monday.

CNBC also reported that a sharp stock price drop after Huang's resignation, along with questions about interim CEO Colette Kress's leadership, played a role in the board’s decision.

Trump's push for Huang's return had the backing of some of Silicon Valley's biggest names.

Timeline of Huang's resignation and return as CEO of Nvidia

By the end of October 2026, scrutiny of Huang had intensified following reports by The New York Times that the woman with whom he had had an affair, Alice Huang, a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was under investigation by US authorities over suspected links to Chinese intelligence. Three Republican House committee chairs sought a closed-door briefing, and the company itself launched an independent investigation on 8 November.

Huang acknowledged that he had been unfaithful to his wife and resigned on 11 November. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress took over as interim CEO. Nvidia's shares closed 4.3% lower the following day, when the company announced his departure.

Growing concerns about Nvidia's future and that of the wider sector triggered a sell-off in AI stocks. Calls for Huang's reinstatement grew increasingly vocal. Tesla CEO Elon Musk backed a petition that had attracted more than 180,000 signatures by 16 November. But during Nvidia's earnings call on 17 November, the board ruled out Huang's return.

The US president entered the debate and publicly made the case for Huang's return on 20 November. Reuters reported that he had sent senior administration officials to pressure the board over the weekend. Directors voted on 22 November, and Nvidia announced the decision on Monday.

Why Huang's return mattered beyond Nvidia

The return of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia gave the equity market a boost unlike anything it had seen in years.

Nvidia shares closed 31.5% higher on Monday, adding almost $1 trillion (€914bn) to its market value. The Nasdaq Composite rose 6.5%, and the S&P 500 gained 4.7%. Bloomberg put the gain in the value of Nasdaq-100 companies at $3tn (€2.74tn) during Monday's session.

The reaction on Wall Street showed how quickly news about Nvidia could move the wider market. The effect on the US economy was harder to estimate. In a November analysis for the Peterson Institute for International Economics, Harvard economist Jason Furman estimated that the data-centre buildout had raised the level of US GDP by about 0.3%, or 0.6% when the associated stock-market boom was included. He also estimated that the buildout had lowered the unemployment rate by about 0.3 percentage points. His conclusion was: "If the stock market gains go away, they could take much of that growth with them".

Huang's resignation added to fears that a stock-market sell-off could wipe out some of the gains the AI boom had brought to the US economy.

Trump cast Huang's return as part of the US race with China for an edge in AI. Huang joined him on a trip to China in May. After a separate meeting with Xi Jinping in November, Trump told CNBC that Xi regarded Huang as the best in the business.

Jensen Huang was widely regarded as an AI evangelist. He had built Nvidia over the previous three decades and developed a business strategy that meant the AI buildout was largely supported by this one company.

Nvidia supplied the chips that powered much of the industry and, with Huang at the helm, helped finance the data centres that used them. In August, Nvidia announced a financing initiative with firms including BlackRock, Brookfield and Goldman Sachs.

Dylan Patel and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis, a semiconductor research firm, argued that smaller cloud providers relied on Huang's backing to raise money. Nvidia could guarantee a minimum level of revenue or back data-centre leases, making it easier for those firms to borrow. After Huang's return, Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said it was still unclear whether Nvidia would continue putting together deals with several partners on the same scale.

The analysis, published after Huang resigned, said the CEO was often the one who had the final say in chip allocation to the hyperscalers and everyone else. Customers had been positioning themselves for allocation and fighting for Nvidia’s attention, and more and more of Nvidia’s deals required extensive Nvidia support.

Nvidia could give more chips to the big cloud companies or to smaller providers, including those in its financing programme. Nvidia helped smaller providers secure financing for their chip clusters in exchange for a share of their cloud revenue. SemiAnalysis argued that Huang's personal backing and appetite for risk-taking made those deals possible.

SemiAnalysis also credited Huang's relationships with suppliers in South Korea and Taiwan, saying that the CEO had personally secured memory supplies in South Korea and chips in Taiwan, "before other executives quite realised how in shortage memory was".

Nvidia's supply and capacity commitments rose from $119 billion (€109bn) to $279bn (€255bn) in its fiscal second quarter. They reached $390bn (€357bn) in the third quarter, with Nvidia attributing the latest increase mainly to multi-year memory purchases.

Huang mattered to clients, too. Reuters reported that after Huang's resignation, some Chinese customers cancelled orders or hesitated to place new ones. Huang had pushed for greater access to the Chinese market, where US controls restricted sales of advanced chips.

Huang was also an outspoken supporter of open AI models, which gave governments, businesses and smaller cloud providers a reason to buy Nvidia chips and run AI themselves.

Congress still has questions for Huang

Lawmakers from both parties criticised the decision to reinstate Huang as Nvidia CEO. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren said Nvidia still owed Congress answers about its compliance with US export controls. Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's return left unanswered questions about national security and unaccounted-for chips.

Democratic Representative Madeleine Dean said Huang's return raised serious questions about national security and how Nvidia was run. “This will not end well for Mr. Huang,” she told Bloomberg Television. Dean sat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, which was due to question Huang behind closed doors on 1 December.

Huang was due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee on 3 December for a public hearing on US export controls. Nvidia's independent investigation remained open.

Two hacking groups extracted the data from the statistics agency's systems on 1 November. The figure comes from death certificates registered up to the end of August, so it excludes missing servicemen and deaths not yet recorded.

A hack of Russia's federal statistics agency Rosstat has revealed that at least 490,000 Russian military personnel have been killed in Ukraine since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to data obtained by hackers and analysed by multiple independent news outlets.

Two hacking groups, Cyber Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow — which also carried out a 2025 attack on Aeroflot's servers — extracted the data in a breach on the night of 1 November.

The hackers accessed Rosstat's electronic document management system and database, which contains around 23 terabytes of statistical, economic and personal data, including census materials.

The figure of at least 490,000 deaths derives from official death certificates registered between February 2022 and the end of August 2026.

Meduza, applying actuarial and epidemiological modelling to the data, estimated at least 720,000 irrecoverable losses when it includes those missing in action. Rosstat's documents alone cannot capture the full toll, as the database does not include servicemen whose deaths have not yet been registered.

Researchers and journalists justify including the missing in total loss figures because, according to Mediazona, confirmed survival is recorded in fewer than 10% of missing servicemen cases.

Under current battlefield conditions, with drone warfare making the evacuation of bodies increasingly difficult, the death tally is likely to grow.

Deaths are also registered with an average delay of 3.5 months, and those of missing soldiers with a delay of about a year, Novaya Evropa reported.

Using the conservative estimate of 490,000 to 500,000 dead, Russia sustained an average of 280 to 300 fatalities a day — one death every five minutes — according to Important Stories, which examined the leak alongside more than a dozen other independent outlets.

The outlet found that 92% of Russian servicemen died from explosions and shrapnel, with firearms accounting for only 1.3% of deaths. The Insider identified more than 370,000 of the dead by name.

The BBC Russian Service and Mediazona said at least 7,421 foreigners have been killed fighting on Russia's side.

Suicides, alcohol and drug use prevalent

Journalists also analysed deaths among Russian servicemen from non-combat causes. Around 2,500 died as a result of alcohol and drug use or suicide.

According to confidential Rosstat data analysed by the international news outlets, more than 1,000 Russian servicemen took their own lives since the start of the invasion.

The deaths of another 885 soldiers in Ukraine or near its borders were registered as firearm injuries "with undetermined intent," a classification experts believe is used in some cases to conceal suicides.

Together, the two figures represent a number comparable to a full Russian regiment.

Military analysts note the problem is deepened in the Russian armed forces by intense pressure from fellow soldiers and commanders, fear of assignment to high-casualty fighting areas known as "meatgrinder assaults," and contracts that in practice prevent soldiers from leaving the war.

Toll highest away from Moscow

The number of Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine is the highest in Russia's Far East and Siberia relative to their populations.

Russia's Jewish Autonomous Region in the Far East recorded nearly 1,000 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, Zabaykalsky around 800, Chukotka 760 and Tuva 650.

Moscow, which the authorities have worked to insulate from the visible effects of the war, recorded 63 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, according to Important Stories.

The Kremlin does not publish or recognise figures for Russian losses from the invasion. Russian authorities have restricted access to official databases and prosecuted those conducting independent counts.

Ukraine's General Staff estimated Russia's losses since February 2022 at 1,639,641 servicemen, encompassing both killed and wounded, although the figure has not been independently verified.

The Economist, in a study published at the end of October, put the number of Russian servicemen killed at between 374,000 and 770,000, and total losses including the wounded at between 1.4 and 2.1 million.

The Ukrainian armed forces' General Staff reported that October of this year was the bloodiest month for Russia since the invasion began.

The Insider said the Russian armed forces suffered their heaviest losses in spring 2025, during fighting on the Pokrovsk axis, when more than 61,000 were killed over three months.

The discovery makes the quasar, extremely bright galactic cores powered by giant black holes, the most distant one ever recorded.

Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its centre dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

The quasar formed within 630 million years of the universe-forming Big Bang, a German-led team reported Tuesday. That's considered a very early development in the 13.8 billion-year history of the cosmos, and it smashes previous records.

“This time the leap in cosmic time is huge!” the European Southern Observatory’s Julien Wolf, who led the study, said in an email. “The previous two records each took us back by about 15 million years or less. This one takes us back by nearly 40 million years, the biggest advance in nearly a decade!”

Wolf and his team spotted the quasar while digging through millions of observations made by the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope. Launched in 2023, Euclid is surveying galaxies in an effort to shed light on the dark matter and dark energy that fill so much of the universe and keep it expanding.

Finding a quasar so early in the universe is rare, according to Wolf. What makes this one even rarer, he said, is the massive size of its black hole, despite being such a relatively slow eater of everything around it. Scientists are seeing it as it was 13.1 billion years ago — when the universe was less than 5% of its current age.

Wolf nicknamed the quasar Dun Aonghasa after the prehistoric stone fort in Ireland's Aran Islands. His wife and daughter are Irish, and he was awestruck when they visited the fort — a frontier holding “the promise of a vast horizon still to explore,” just like this quasar.

His team's findings were corroborated by the Hubble and Webb space telescopes as well as other observatories on and off Earth. Thanks to Webb, scientists learned that the black hole powering this quasar is equivalent in mass to 360 million of our suns, an astounding amount so early in time. The final results appear in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

“Dun Aonghasa gives us a new deadline” for the early universe, Wolf said. “About 630 million years after the Big Bang, its black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun. But how?”

Their prowling of the cosmic dawn continues.

“Honestly, the record could fall again in a few months or it could stand for years,” Wolf said.

Judges reversed an earlier downgrade of the charge, ruling that a shot to the chest fired from 16cm pointed to an intent to kill. The officer now faces up to 30 years in prison.

The Versailles Court of Appeal in France ruled on Tuesday that Florian M., the police officer who shot dead Nahel Merzouk on 27 June 2023, should stand trial for murder before an assize court.

He faces up to 30 years in prison, which would have been capped at 15 years for violence resulting in death without intent to kill, before any aggravating circumstances are taken into account.

Florian M. will therefore be tried by an assize court with a lay jury, rather than by a criminal court made up exclusively of professional judges.

The ruling comes after a series of legal twists in a case that has become a symbol of police violence.

On 27 June 2023, Nahel Merzouk, 17, was killed in Nanterre, in the Hauts-de-Seine department, when Florian M. shot him at point-blank range during a traffic stop. The scene was filmed and widely shared on social media, and it led to several nights of violence across France.

After a two-year investigation, two investigating judges ordered the officer to stand trial for murder before the Hauts-de-Seine assize court, in line with the recommendation of the Nanterre public prosecutor's office.

Florian M., who spent five months in pre-trial detention before being released, appealed against the decision.

In March, the investigating chamber of the Versailles Court of Appeal reclassified the case. It ordered the officer to stand trial before the Hauts-de-Seine departmental criminal court on the lesser charge of violence resulting in death without intent to kill, to the dismay of Nahel's family, who are civil parties in the case.

In their ruling, the judges found the evidence "insufficient" to establish that Florian M. had intended to kill. They also upheld the dismissal of the case against the second police officer present during the traffic stop.

The reclassification satisfied no one. The prosecutor general's office, the civil parties and the defence, which had hoped for the case to be dropped, all appealed to the Court of Cassation, France's highest court.

The question of intent to kill

In a new twist, the Court of Cassation overturned the reclassification in June, once again paving the way for Florian M. to be tried for murder. It also confirmed the dismissal of the case against the other officer.

The Court of Cassation, which rules solely on points of law and not on the facts of a case, found that the appeal court had "not justified its decision" to reclassify the charge.

The case was therefore sent back to the investigating chamber of the Versailles Court of Appeal. In September, a different panel of judges re-examined whether Florian M. had intended to kill.

On Tuesday, the court found that his use of a firearm, the short distance of the shot and the part of the body struck pointed to an intent to kill. The shot was fired 16cm from the windscreen of the car Nahel was driving, and it hit him in the chest, a vital area.

The ruling, which was delivered behind closed doors, can still be appealed. Franck Berton, the lawyer for Nahel's mother, had argued that the officer should stand trial for murder. The officer's lawyer, Laurent-Franck Liénard, had declined to comment before the ruling.

Before Tuesday's decision, the Justice for Nahel committee, of which his mother Mounia Merzouk is a member, had called on the court to deliver a "firm decision" by upholding the murder charge. Louise Tort, who represents several members of the family, said they had been waiting "impatiently" for the ruling.

The judgment from the European Court of Human Rights concerns separate incidents from 2021, when Belarus facilitated the movement of irregular migrants towards EU borders as a means of exerting political pressure, prompting Polish and Latvian authorities to intercept and immediately return them.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled on Tuesday that Polish and Latvian authorities subjected individuals from Afghanistan and Iraq who tried to enter their territory from Belarus to inhuman or degrading treatment, potentially setting a precedent against summary pushbacks by EU countries.

The ruling covers separate cases dating back to 2021, when irregular migrants used by Belarus as a tool of political pressure were intercepted at the border and summarily turned back.

The decision was highly awaited, as it is the first to address the protection of people caught up in the instrumentalisation of migration. It could set a precedent for similar cases of state-sponsored pressure, such as the mass arrival of irregular migrants in Ceuta from Morocco last July.

The first case concerned two Afghan nationals who crossed the Polish border from Belarus illegally and were left stranded in a makeshift camp on Polish territory between August and October 2021, before being pushed back across the border into Belarus.

In the second, 19 Iraqi nationals of Kurdish origin, including six children, accused Latvia of pushing them back into Belarus after an irregular border crossing in August 2021.

Both situations occurred in the context of hostile actions by the Belarusian authorities, described as "instrumentalisation of migration". Minsk had encouraged, facilitated or forced the movement of migrants across its borders with EU countries to destabilise neighbouring states.

The Court held that countries have the right to control the entry of foreign nationals into their territory, and that removing irregular migrants to the instrumentalising state would not, in itself, violate Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment.

However, national authorities must identify people who are particularly vulnerable to ill-treatment, including elderly, disabled or sick individuals, as well as anyone facing a clear and immediate risk of such treatment.

As a result, the court found violations only in the cases of some applicants: one Afghan national who entered Poland, and all the children who crossed into Latvia, along with their accompanying family members.

The Court stated that children must be treated as an extremely vulnerable group with specific needs and therefore cannot be pushed back, even in cases of instrumentalisation.

Another case against Lithuania, concerning four Cuban nationals who repeatedly crossed the Lithuanian-Belarusian border in 2022, was rejected. The Court found no violation of Article 3.

ECHR judgments are legally binding under the Convention, with their implementation overseen by the Council of Europe, a separate organisation from the EU that brings together 46 European countries.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen drew sharp criticism after making controversial remarks on migration in a domestic podcast, emphasising Denmark's "ethnically Danish" population and appearing to echo the far-right "great replacement" theory.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen's hardline stance on migration has fuelled a growing rift within the European Parliament's S&D group, putting her Socialdemokratiet party at odds with its centre-left allies.

On Tuesday, the S&D leader Iratxe García Pérez said the group would hold internal discussions on the issue "as soon as possible", after several MEPs brought it up during a group meeting.

“There is no doubt about the positions defended by our political family. The respect of international law is a crucial element,” she said.

Frederiksen sparked a backlash with recent comments on migration in a domestic podcast, touting the “ethnically Danish origin” of her country's population and even echoing the “great replacement” theory, a far-right conspiracy theory alleging a plot to dilute Europe’s white population.

“This podcast was a disaster,” an S&D MEP told Euronews on condition of anonymity, summing up a widespread view in the group.

Copenhagen has adopted one of the EU's toughest approaches to irregular migration, joining forces with right-wing governments, including Italy and Belgium to advance its agenda.

Notably, Denmark is one of five EU countries that struck a partnership with Rwanda to deport irregular migrants to the first-ever return hub outside the bloc. The S&D group has campaigned against the EU law enabling return hubs, called the “return regulation,” and voted overwhelmingly against it in the European Parliament last June.

“We can open up again an internal debate on migration policy. But the group already has a position on return hubs: they have no legal ground and are not in line with international law,” García Pérez said at a press conference the same day.

She said the majority of the group opposes the Danish line on migration, a claim confirmed to Euronews by S&D MEPs from other countries.

“For now, no one is taking [Frederisken’s] side”, a senior Socialist lawmaker told Euronews.

Another MEP likened her statements on migration to the “worst propaganda from [Italian Prime Minister] Giorgia Meloni.”

Only a few S&D lawmakers, from Malta, Romania, Latvia and Sweden, broke ranks with the group’s line by voting in favour or abstaining on the return regulation. But none of them has so far spoken out in defence of Frederiksen’s stance, according to several sources in the group.

The discussion will probably take place in the coming weeks, after the Strasbourg plenary session, according to an S&D official.

Although Denmark's position conflicts with the group's stance, no sanctions or concrete action are currently expected, as any decision on the matter would need to be taken at a higher political level.

Any disciplinary measures against Danish S&D members could be considered only within the Party of European Socialists (PES), the European centre-left umbrella party whose parliamentary expression is the S&D group, García Pérez said.

Euronews reached out to the Danish S&D delegation for comment, but had not received a response at the time of publication.

In the Maldives, farmers grow crops on nutrient-poor coral sand. Thousands of kilometres away, Uzbekistan monitors farmland from space. Despite their different environments, both countries are finding ways to tackle a major challenge: producing food with limited resources.

On a tropical island in the Indian Ocean, banana trees, papayas and chillies are thriving where farming seems almost impossible. The soil is little more than coral sand, freshwater is scarce, and most of the country's food arrives from overseas.

This is the Maldives, an archipelago famous for its white-sand beaches and luxury resorts. But beyond the postcard coastline lies a serious problem: how to feed a nation with almost no land fit for farming.

In landlocked Uzbekistan, the problem is reversed: there is land in abundance, but the water to farm it is running short.

Their solutions differ sharply, but both are tackling a question that reaches far beyond their borders: how to keep food on the table as environmental pressures intensify.

A farm in paradise

According to the United Nations, nearly 90% of the Maldives' food is imported, and just 27 square kilometres of land across the archipelago can be cultivated.

That leaves the island nation at the mercy of global supply chains and rising food prices.

Coral sand is naturally alkaline, contains few nutrients and lets water drain straight through, making conventional farming a constant struggle. On South Ari Atoll, the Villa Park resort is proving it can still be done.

On three to four hectares, some of it once underwater, the resort has built a farm producing bananas, papayas, chillies, curry leaves and more. Some of the harvest even reaches local markets several times a week.

One of the secrets to turning barren sand into productive ground is surprisingly simple: compost.

"We grow the things in here with the sand, but we have enriched the sand with our own compost," says Raminda Premaratne, Director of Culinary at Villa Park.

For Premaratne, the benefits go beyond the farm itself. Fruit and vegetables imported into the Maldives often travel long distances, and not all of it survives the journey.

"When we import lots of fruits and vegetables from other countries, we get a lot of wastage and spoilage at the end," Premaratne says.

Growing on the island shrinks the journey from farm to plate to a short walk and cuts the resort's reliance on shipments.

The Villa Group, which owns the resort, is even experimenting with apples and oranges, pushing the limits of what the island can grow. For its chairman, Qasim Ibrahim, local food production is both an environmental ambition and a response to the vulnerabilities of island life.

Yet the project has limits. Villa Park is large by Maldivian standards, and on many resort islands there simply isn't enough space for agriculture on this scale.

Still, it shows that even the most unpromising land can help build a more resilient food supply.

Monitoring agriculture from space

Agriculture accounts for around 90% of Uzbekistan's water consumption. The World Bank projects that water availability could fall by 30 to 40% in some river basins by 2050, while irrigation demand in summer could rise by as much as 25%.

To keep a closer eye on its farmland, Uzbekistan's space agency, Uzcosmos, is turning to satellites.

Its satellites have surveyed more than four million hectares, allowing specialists to identify crops, follow their development and detect changes in individual fields without setting foot in them.

A second project follows the water itself.

"In this project, we digitise the entire irrigation network, from the main water sources down to smaller irrigation and drainage channels, and link them to the fields being irrigated," says Sharof Boltayev, Chief Specialist at Uzcosmos.

The agency is also estimating how much water each plot consumes. More than ten ground-monitoring devices in the Fergana and Samarkand regions verify the satellite estimates against readings taken on the ground.

The aim is to pinpoint where water is being wasted and give farmers a clearer picture of their land.

Farming without soil

Near Tashkent, scientists at the Research Institute of Vegetable, Melon Crops and Potato are testing hydroponics, a technique in which plants grow without any soil at all.

Instead, crops are held in a growing substrate, while water and dissolved nutrients are delivered directly to their roots through drip irrigation.

According to Fakhriddin Rasulov, the institute's Scientific Secretary, the main advantage is precision: growers can control exactly how much water and fertiliser their plants receive. The method can also be used on rocky terrain or other land unsuitable for conventional cultivation.

Researchers are testing locally developed strawberry and tomato varieties, with the aim of developing methods that could eventually be recommended to farmers. In separate experiments, the institute is studying how unheated greenhouses can deliver two or three harvests a year from the same plot.

Such systems still require investment, energy and specialist expertise. But where traditional farming is running up against its limits, they offer another way forward.

Different challenges, a shared future

Neither compost on coral sand nor satellites over Uzbek farmland is a universal solution. But together, they point to a broader shift: the future of food may depend less on growing more, and more on making the most of what each environment can offer.

The report highlights how health inequalities affect children from disadvantaged backgrounds, shaping their development and opportunities from the earliest stages of life.

Across the European region, an estimated 187 million people – around one in five – are living in poor health due to health and social inequality, according to the World Health Organization.

“Across our region, people are living longer, healthier lives. Many countries have made real gains in social protection, education, jobs and access to care. But here is the uncomfortable truth: progress isn't reaching everyone,” said Corinne Capuano, officer-in-charge at WHO’s Europe office, during a press briefing presenting the report.

While overall life expectancy and health have improved across generations, that progress is uneven, the authors said.

Inequalities start in childhood

Children are among those particularly affected by health inequalities. An estimated 35 million children and adolescents across the 53 countries of the WHO European Region, which spans Europe and Central Asia, are held back by avoidable health and social inequities, the report found.

Those in the poorest households are twice as likely to die before age five and six times as likely to face severe housing deprivation compared to those in the richest households.

The report identified several groups that are particularly vulnerable, including Roma children, children with disabilities or neurodevelopmental conditions, adolescent girls, and those from less-educated families or living in disadvantaged neighbourhoods.

Girls from low-income families were in worse health in 91% of countries; for boys, that figure was 96%. Overall, girls report poorer health than boys in almost every country, regardless of household income.

Health inequities take root during childhood and adolescence, shaping people’s development, educational attainment and future opportunities long before adulthood, the WHO warned. The first 1,000 days of life are particularly important to prevent disadvantages from becoming rooted over a lifetime, the organization said.

The report found that early investments in family support, nutrition, housing and early learning can yield up to an eightfold return on investment over a child's lifetime.

What drives inequalities?

The report found that the main drivers of health inequity are non-medical living costs and socioeconomic conditions, including low wages, food insecurity, inadequate pensions, poor job conditions and unsafe housing.

In childhood, these inequalities are driven largely by child poverty, barriers to early learning and education, adverse social circumstances such as bullying at school or online, and unequal access to health services.

“Too often, where you are born, what your family earns and whether you can find decent work or training still dictate how healthy you will be,” Capuano said.

Geographical differences

Western Europe saw the biggest gaps, with girls showing the greatest progress while boys experienced the greatest deterioration in equality over the 12-year study period between 2010 and 2022.

Northern Europe recorded the least overall progress, with inequalities stagnating among girls and worsening among boys.

Health gaps narrowed the fastest in Eastern Europe.

“If countries are serious about closing the health gap, three things need to happen now,” Natasha Azzopardi-Muscat, director of health systems at WHO’s Europe office, told Euronews in a written comment.

That includes ensuring low-income people can access affordable healthcare when they need it, assessing the health impact of any budget cuts on the most vulnerable before they are made, and pairing social benefits with clear pathways into work, education and decent housing.

The report's recommendations also include ensuring both parents have access to well-paid, non-transferable parental leave; providing free or subsidised school meals and breakfasts; and introducing evidence-based, whole-school anti-bullying programmes.

“Closing the gap eases pressure on health services, strengthens economies and holds our societies together,” Azzopardi-Muscat said.

EU capitals are divided on several fronts ahead of key talks on the bloc's next long-term budget: overall size, political priorities, Ukraine financing and new EU taxes. Tense domestic politics make compromise harder, with only leaders expected to break the deadlock.

National deficits, political manoeuvring and the cost of supporting Ukraine are making the EU's budget negotiations increasingly difficult. Member states face the delicate task of balancing competing demands while keeping negotiations on track.

On Saturday, European Council President António Costa made a bold move to break the deadlock over the bloc's next seven-year budget, known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), ahead of a special European Council summit starting on Thursday.

Costa's proposal cuts the overall volume further, touches cohesion funding for the first time, introduces a new digital levy and partly rolls over the joint debt under the EU's post-pandemic recovery fund. Member states responded with the usual bashing.

At a meeting of EU ambassadors, known as COREPER, on Monday, "many states said that it is not a basis for compromise and that we are getting further away," said an EU diplomat who, like others quoted in this article, spoke with Euronews on condition of anonymity.

"Yesterday's COREPER discussion showed this file needs to be dealt with at the leaders' level," a second EU diplomat told Euronews. "It was pretty bad, four hours of discussion with no practical outcome."

Public spats have become a fixture of EU budget talks, blurring the lines between negotiating tactics and actual positions as member states dig in their heels.

Overall size

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called Costa's proposal a "first step", a relatively mild reaction compared with that of the German ambassador, who was far more vocal at COREPER and rejected it as a basis for discussion.

Berlin and the other so-called "frugal countries", net contributors such as the Netherlands and Sweden, want a further cut to the overall volume.

In current prices, Costa trimmed the budget by €204bn compared with the Commission's original proposal. In real terms, the cut is a more modest €181bn.

Roughly €10bn of that comes from delaying repayment of NextGenerationEU, which the frugals see not as a reduction but as kicking the can down the road.

Despite the visceral opposition of countries like the Netherlands and Germany to more joint debt, the proposed delay drew little pushback, as it is seen as the lesser evil. Still, another €30bn in real terms is necessary to reach the €200bn threshold.

But how much cutting is enough? The frugals have no common position and prefer a vague call for "several hundred billion euros". In practice, that may only be settled at the last minute through national rebates.

Political priorities

An Élysée Palace source was quick to dismiss Costa's proposal as "very disappointing", and said it "does not constitute a basis for an agreement" primarily because it failed to guarantee income support for farmers.

France's stance baffled other capitals. Paris has already won considerable concessions, including the digital levy and an untouched Common Agricultural Policy envelope.

The frugals prefer to call themselves the "modernisers". They argue the EU budget should focus on emerging priorities such as defence, migration and innovation, which have instead borne the brunt of the cuts.

Costa did touch cohesion funding for the first time, but the frugals regard the cut as largely symbolic, a result of opposition from a 17-strong "Friends of Cohesion" group led by Italy and Romania.

For the frugals, a rebalancing of spending is needed to reflect the new geopolitical reality.

"Central and Eastern European countries are still not able to prioritise between traditional policies and investment in resilience and security. It means others will do it for them. It will strengthen the South's systematic efforts for prioritising cohesion over regions close to Russia," a third EU diplomat told Euronews.

Ukraine support

Merz has linked the budget talks to financial support for Kyiv. Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria, which want to opt out of the upcoming top-up of the Ukraine Support Loan, are also staunch defenders of cohesion policy.

The move prompted a fierce backlash from the four leaders. Slovakia's Prime Minister Robert Fico branded Merz's tactic "blackmail" and threatened to use Slovakia's veto to block the budget.

"The fact that MFF and Ukraine are in parallel is almost obvious, even if many don't like it. The important thing is that one does not put the other at risk, but in reality, it will," a fourth diplomat told Euronews.

A possible compromise would let the countries that want out do so for the military part, worth €25bn, while still backing the civilian part, the remaining €20bn.

"The European Commission is doing a lot of creative thinking on the financing of Ukraine. There is a sense of optimism," the second diplomat said.

EU-wide taxes

A key novelty in Costa's proposal is an EU-wide levy on digital services, to replace an extremely controversial corporate tax.

The digital levy did not receive strong opposition from member states, except Ireland, home to most of the European headquarters of US tech companies. The main argument against it is the risk of trade retaliation from Washington.

The Commission first proposed a digital services tax in 2018, and France, Italy and Spain have national versions in place. But EU countries are wary that the digital economy has changed significantly since then, so the proposal needs to be refined.

Several other EU-wide taxes to finance the budget, known as own resources, still face significant opposition. That is notably true of the Emissions Trading System (ETS), strongly opposed by the likes of Poland and Bulgaria.

Again, willingness to accept new own resources that cost some countries more than average may only be secured in the final stretch, when leaders push for country-specific concessions elsewhere.

Complicated context

The tension is not confined to Brussels. With interest rates rising, energy prices high and deficits ballooning under the weight of public spending and support for Ukraine, many member states feel the budget heat at home.

In Belgium, the government's survival is at stake after coalition talks on the 2027 budget collapsed. In the Netherlands, the minority government faces a serious political crisis over a tax package tied to the national budget.

Romania's government collapsed in May, and the country is running a deficit close to 8%. In France, budget disputes have been a major driver of instability for two years.

Overall, 10 of 27 member states are in an excessive deficit procedure, and the Commission estimates the number could rise to 16 after next year, based on projected spending.

Upcoming national elections in key countries such as France, Italy and Poland, along with the rise of extreme forces on both ends of the political spectrum in regional elections in countries like Germany, are hardening governments' stances.

"Political and economic context is very difficult, and that makes it very difficult for different member states to compromise," the fourth EU diplomat added.

China is encouraging more trade and investment in yuan, although the currency remains far less widely used than the dollar. Singapore’s new financing plans would give businesses more ways to access yuan, including funding for trade with other countries.

China and Singapore have agreed to expand yuan financing for businesses, including funding for trade involving other countries, as Beijing seeks wider international use of its currency.

The measures were announced on Monday at the Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation meeting in Singapore, co-chaired by Singapore’s Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong and Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang.

They form part of 29 agreements and cooperation initiatives covering areas including finance, trade, technology and healthcare. The package includes new agreements, renewals of existing arrangements and proposals for further work.

Singapore’s central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), and the People’s Bank of China will restructure an existing yuan funding scheme backed by an agreement between the two central banks to exchange currencies.

One programme will allow eligible financial institutions to obtain yuan for a wider range of business lending, including trade involving other countries, daily operating costs and investment. Funding will be available for one, three or six months.

A second programme will continue to provide backup yuan funding to financial institutions in Singapore. The range of assets accepted as security for borrowing will also expand, while accepting Chinese government bonds remains under discussion.

The central banks are also exploring a link between their fast payment systems for small transfers between the two countries. MAS did not announce an increase in the total funding available.

China’s push for wider yuan use

The changes come as China encourages more businesses to use the yuan, also known as the renminbi, for international trade and investment.

An August analysis by the Reserve Bank of Australia said wider use could help China reduce the financial and geopolitical risks associated with reliance on the US dollar.

The share of China’s trade settled in yuan had risen from below 20% in 2021 to around 35%, the analysis found. However, there was little evidence of widespread yuan use in trade that did not involve China.

The currency also accounted for less than 2% of global foreign exchange reserves, well behind the dollar and euro. Restrictions on moving money across China’s borders and its less developed financial markets remain obstacles to wider use, the Australian central bank said.

The financial measures build on existing links. DBS has begun yuan clearing services, helping banks process payments in the currency. Singapore and China also plan to support companies seeking stock market listings and funding in each other’s markets.

Beyond finance, the countries announced plans for an economic corridor linking Singapore, Tianjin Eco-City and Xiong’an New Area in northern China.

Singapore’s National Development Minister Chee Hong Tat said the aim was to help companies from the Tianjin region use Singapore as a base for expansion into Southeast Asia, while opening opportunities in China for Singaporean businesses.

The meeting followed Friday’s announcement of negotiations to upgrade the China–Singapore free trade agreement. Those talks will cover the digital economy and government procurement, with Singapore also seeking to make cross-border data transfers easier.

Pesticide exposure may affect people’s fertility, but more conclusive research is needed.

Pesticide exposure may harm fertility, experts warned as the European Union weighs simpler rules on how pesticides are approved.

About one in six people worldwide experiences infertility, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Lifestyle factors such as smoking, heavy drinking and obesity can raise the risk of infertility, while exposure to pesticides and other environmental pollutants has been linked to poorer sperm and egg quality.

Pesticide exposure may affect people’s fertility by interfering with their hormones and reproductive cells, a pair of Italian endocrinologists warned at a briefing organised by the Brussels nonprofit Health and Environment Alliance (HEAL).

In men, infertility is commonly caused by low sperm counts, abnormal shape or movement of the sperm, or issues with semen ejaculation, according to the WHO. Chemical exposures can disrupt testicular function and sperm maturation through oxidative stress, endocrine disruption and direct damage to reproductive cells, which may affect fertility.

In 2023, researchers found that men with more exposure to certain insecticides, mostly through work, tended to have lower sperm concentrations.

The results of other studies are mixed, but the findings are enough to worry experts.

“There is a close relationship between male fertility and sperm quality,” said Dr. Aldo Calogero, an endocrinology professor at the University of Catania.

In women, infertility is typically caused by problems with the ovaries, uterus, fallopian tubes or endocrine system, according to the WHO.

Because women are born with all of the eggs they will ever produce, researchers suspect that pesticide exposure before birth may matter more than in adulthood. Pesticide exposure during pregnancy has also been linked to poorer brain development in their developing foetuses.

Pregnancy is “a very fundamental timing of our life when we can effectively reduce the exposure to several chemicals in order to protect the health of the offspring, even the reproductive health,” said Dr. Rossella Cannarella, an endocrinology specialist at the same university.

EU policymakers are now considering new legislation to simplify food and feed safety rules, including the approval of pesticides. The proposal aims to cut bureaucratic red tape for farmers and national authorities, according to the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm.
