The number of victims of domestic violence was higher in 2025 than ever before, according to new reports from the Federal Criminal Police Office. Violence against women and girls has risen across many categories of offences.

In 2026 at least 125 women were killed in Germany. They were killed by men with whom they were in, or had been in, relationships in which love was supposed to play a role, but which ultimately turned out to be a patriarchal form of gender-based violence.

At least 126 other women survived an attempted femicide in 2025. This is the conclusion reached by the alliance Keine*Mehr alliance, which is calling for protests on 25 November the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.

The Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) does not record femicide as a separate offence, but reports that 209 women died as a result of domestic violence in 2025, 130 of whom were killed by a current or former partner. In total, 292 people died as a result of domestic violence. There is also a newly established federal-state working group that is developing a definition of femicide and is to collect specific information on it in future.

"Almost every day in Germany a man kills his partner or ex-partner, or tries to," Federal Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig (SPD) told Bild am Sonntag. But not every one of these acts was clearly classified as murder, and there is still no official public statistic on femicides. Hubig wants to change that: the Criminal Code's provision on murder is to be expanded to include femicides.

Femicide to be treated as murder in future

A killing is considered a femicide when a man kills a woman because she separates from him or wants to make her own decisions about her life. There is not yet a legally clear definition. In future, "gender-specific or other inhuman motives" should explicitly be listed as aggravating features of murder, according to the draft bill by the Justice Minister reported by Bild am Sonntag.

Until now, many femicide cases have been classified in court as manslaughter. In legal terms both manslaughter and murder are intentional killings. However, the motives in murder are considered especially reprehensible, including for example killing for pleasure, treachery, cruelty and base motives. This can affect the sentence. Under the new draft bill, killing a (former) partner is to be classified as murder in all cases, no longer as manslaughter.

"Women must be safe from violence and assaults, no matter where and how they are out and about, what opinions they express and what life decisions they make," Hubig stressed at an event on the topic. This is still far from the reality: "Violence and assaults against women are a massive problem in Germany, in partnerships and families, in public spaces and in the digital world," Hubig added.

Situation reports: increases in almost all offence categories

In the past year 54,675 women and girls were recorded as victims of sexual offences, an increase of 2.3% compared with the previous year. Almost half of them were minors at the time of the offence. This is shown by the situation reports published on Tuesday by the Federal Criminal Police Office. In the area of digital violence, such as coercion, threats and stalking, the number of female victims rose by almost 16% compared with the previous year.

"The federal situation reports show that violence against women is a problem in Germany. Far too often women are threatened, abused, humiliated and killed," said Hubig. "We must protect those affected better, hold perpetrators consistently to account and prevent violence at an early stage," said Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt. Concrete support services are to be strengthened so that previously hidden violence also becomes visible.

The figures on domestic violence include both partner violence and violence within the family. Both categories have more victims than in the previous year. Victims of domestic violence are predominantly female at 70.6%, and in cases of partnership violence the share of female victims is even higher at 79.4%.

Federal Women’s Affairs Minister Karin Prien and Hubig both emphasise that further measures, such as tougher penalties for date-rape drugs, electronic ankle bracelets for offenders and strengthening women’s shelters and prevention work, are to be implemented. "And we need a rethink in society, a break with outdated images of masculinity and patriarchal patterns of thought," Hubig concluded.

The proportion of offences reported to the police is below 10% for most of the forms of violence examined, according to further information from the BKA. The study also shows that only 3% of women report sexual assaults.

Sexualised violence against women is everyday reality

The alliance Keine* Mehr and other associations point out that this is a systemic problem. "They know what they are doing," said the organisation Terre des Femmes in a call for protests on Wednesday. According to this, perpetrators drug women in order to rape them while they are unconscious. This sexualised violence and so-called chemical submission is the focus of Terre des Femmes this year.

Just a few weeks ago a perpetrator was convicted at the Berlin Regional Court who, over more than a decade, invited women to his home, drugged them, raped them, filmed the assaults and then shared the recordings on the internet. There was hardly any sign of remorse, on the contrary, the judges spoke of a deliberate exploitation of the imbalance of power.

One in two women experiences partner violence

One in two women experiences violence from her partner at least once in her life, whether psychological, physical, sexual or digital. This was the finding of the LeSuBia dark-figure study by the Federal Criminal Police Office, published in February 2026. While many people picture a partner who beats them, systematically ignoring "no" during sexual acts or devaluing and insulting a partner are also forms of violence.

"Violence against women is not a problem of a lack of caution. It is a problem of violent men," said Nastassja Wachsmuth, Director of Communications and Foundation at Terre des Femmes. Together with the advertising agency KNSK, the organisation has launched the awareness campaign "Every second woman".

View this post on Instagram

"Partner violence is not an invisible fringe phenomenon, it is a reality at the heart of our society," said Kim Notz, owner of KNSK. "We place the socially romanticised picture of relationship happiness directly alongside the bitter reality of violence," Notz continued. Because while some women are given roses, others receive black eyes, as one of the posters says.

Attitudes towards women still poor

According to an international survey, around one in ten male baby boomers believes a wife must always obey her husband. Among Generation Z it is almost one in three respondents, according to a survey by the polling institute Ipsos from March 2026.

"It is worrying to see that attitudes to gender equality are not more positive, particularly among young men," said Julia Gillard of King’s Business School in London, who was involved in the Ipsos survey. According to the survey, 61% of men born between 1997 and 2012 believe that enough has been done for gender equality. Fifty-seven percent of this group even think that men are now discriminated against. In Germany the figures are 55% and 37% respectively.

"This year’s survey shows us that we may be witnessing a major renegotiation of gender roles in today’s society," said Kelly Beaver, Chief Executive of Ipsos in the United Kingdom and Ireland. According to the survey, young men more often endorse traditional hierarchies in relationships and have a problem when women earn more or act independently.

"Digital ecosystems intensify polarisation because social media algorithms reward pointed messages," from masculinity influencers through to feminist counter-narratives, explained Robert Grimm, Head of Political Research at Ipsos in Germany.

By international comparison, attitudes in Germany are more moderate than average. Only one in ten people in Germany believes that women benefit when men stick to traditional male role models. This is the lowest figure among all 29 countries surveyed, according to Ipsos.

A year after the Washington summit that brought peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project has entered its construction phase amid broader geopolitical reshaping in the region and beyond.

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan announced "the launch of the practical phase" of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), the key regional US-backed transit corridor of the South Caucasus, as Armenia and Azerbaijan continue building together the future of the region after decades of tragic wars.

In his official launch address, Pashinyan described the launch as "a truly historic event in the modern history of the Republic of Armenia,” describing TRIPP as the largest economic project in Armenia since its independence.

"Beyond the benefits of connecting Azerbaijan with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic, and the mutual advantages for the Republic of Armenia in terms of developing international and domestic connectivity, the TRIPP project will hold immense regional and international significance by infusing additional vitality into the Trans-Caspian trade route and West-East connectivity," he added.

Announcing that TRIPP will be "jointly implemented by the Governments of Armenia and the United States,” together with Azerbaijan, Pashinyan said that the initiative aims to establish unimpeded, multimodal transit across the South Caucasus based on full respect for the "sovereignty, territorial integrity, and jurisdiction" of participating states.

Armenia’s prime minister added that the project will enable Yerevan to access foreign markets and attract investment to Armenia’s southern Syunik province. It will also contribute to Armenia's security, with its neighbours seeking stability for the regional developments, according to Pashinyan.

A live television broadcast following his speech showed the start of the preparatory construction in Armenia’s Syunik province, linking mainland Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave.

Syunik governor Robert Ghukasyan confirmed that work began at several locations in the Meghri area, noting that major construction will follow after an initial period of preparatory work.

Pashinyan earlier said electricity transit will be a main component of the project, amid plans to connect Armenia, Azerbaijan and Turkey’s grids in a major geopolitical development for the region.

Another key component is building a railway connecting the project countries, with an agreed completion date of 2028.

Washington's backing and joint development structure

In a video address marking the kickoff, US President Donald Trump congratulated Pashinyan on launching the project and praised his efforts toward peace with Azerbaijan.

Trump announced the establishment of the TRIPP Development Company, stating that the US-Armenia partnership will open new routes for cargo, energy flows, and passenger travel across the South Caucasus.

"Today, we continue our progress with the launch of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity and the brand-new TRIPP Development Company,” Trump said, adding that “this partnership between the United States and Armenia will create new trade routes for the flow of goods, energy, and travel throughout the region.”

“We are committed to ensuring it is a great, great success," Trump said.

Under the bilateral framework ratified by Armenia's parliament in October and signed by President Vahagn Khachaturyan earlier this month Washington holds a 74% stake in the joint operating company and Yerevan holds the remaining 26%, but the agreement's provisions allow Armenia’s share to rise to 49% if the partnership is extended.

Armenian officials pointed out that Yerevan retains control over legislation, customs and administration along the route.

Trump also thanked both Pashinyan and Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev for their cooperation and invited the Armenian premier to visit the White House in 2027, when Pashinyan is scheduled to travel to Washington for the National Prayer Breakfast.

"I once again want to thank Prime Minister Pashinyan and his counterpart, President Aliyev of Azerbaijan, for working with us to make this day possible and for so generously nominating me for the Nobel Peace Prize," he added.

Shortly after the announcement, Azerbaijan's president posted a statement on X thanking Trump for his remarks at the project's launch.

The TRIPP initiative stems from the 8 August 2025 joint declaration signed in Washington by Aliyev and Pashinyan in Trump's presence, where the two countries' foreign ministers launched the two countries’ peace agreement.

Restoring unhindered transport and logistical links between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan has been a central pillar of the normalisation process between Baku and Yerevan.

The TRIPP project is the key component of the wider so-called Middle Corridor, the emerging strategic transit and trade route between Asia and Europe and a strong Eurasian alternative amid global supply chain disruptions in the Middle East.

The Middle Corridor is a rail and maritime transport network that will connect China, Southeast Asia, and Central Asia with European markets via the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus to the Black Sea.

Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan are stepping up their cooperation to develop the Middle Corridor, as the network will pass through these countries and onwards to Turkey and Europe, through a joint plan aimed at improving transport infrastructure, streamlining logistics, and making cross-border trade faster and more efficient.

The joint plan comes as European companies explore new investment opportunities along the route.

The participating countries are discussing how to connect the energy routes and markets from a so-called strategic-geography perspective, with significant political and economic benefits and growing influence.

The US-backed project is moving forward in a complex geopolitical area marked by tensions, with Iran and Russia following closely.

Both the TRIPP project and the wider Middle Corridor face geopolitical challenges, depending on the ongoing peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia, notably Armenia’s adoption of its peace treaty through a new constitution, as well as the possible challenges posed by Iran and Russia to the US-backed TRIPP project and the wider interactions of the participating countries within the current geopolitical reshaping processes.

The rule change will mean pet owners no longer need to fork out for an animal health certificate each time they travel.

Travelling to the EU with cats, dogs and ferrets as a Brit is about to get easier – and cheaper – thanks to the reintroduction of pet passports.

From 1 March 2028, pet owners will be able to get a multiuse passport which is valid for EU travel rather than securing a new animal health certificate for each trip.

The details around how to get a multiuse pet passport will be shared in 2027. You can sign up for updates on the UK government website (or keep your eyes peeled on Euronews Travel).

The British Veterinary Association said in a statement: “This new agreement is broadly positive news and one that we've been pressing the UK government for. But it is important that the transition to the new trade rules is smooth and doesn’t negatively impact vets working across all parts of the profession.”

The news comes after the UK and EU agreed to align on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) rules, with a number of other changes introduced.

Cats, dogs and ferrets microchipped from 1 March 2028 will need to have a code that shows the country where the animal was initially identified. This will not apply retroactively.

The UK is also set to work to ensure its microchip database system works with EU systems.

What are the current rules for travelling with pets to the EU?

Following the closure of a loophole in April that allowed Brits with holiday homes in EU countries to continue to use EU pet passports from before Brexit, all cats, dogs and ferrets have needed an animal health certificate to travel to the EU.

To get the health certificate, your pet must have either an up-to-date rabies vaccination or only need booster doses to keep the vaccination up to date. You’ll also need to take proof of your pet’s microchipping date, and vaccination history.

The certificate will be valid for 10 days, with day one being the date it is issued. It will also be valid for six months for onward travel within the EU after entering, as well as for re-entry into Great Britain.

Pets who need a rabies vaccination will need to wait for it to work, which could take as long as 30 days, before the certificate can be issued.

Only official veterinarians can sign the certificates, and prices can vary between £90 (€108) and £250 (€299), depending on factors like turnaround times and vet location.

The new orbital economy is worth billions and increasingly involves private operators. Europe is seeking a strategy to avoid losing ground.

Forty-five countries gathered in Rome to discuss who will write the future rules for space. It is a race in which the United States and China are sprinting ahead, private players are gaining ground and Europe still has to close the gap in its capacity for autonomous access to orbit. This is the backdrop to the eighth edition of the International Space Forum, returning to Italy ten years after its debut in Trento.

The numbers show how crowded the race has become. In 2026 there are about 18,000 operational satellites around the Earth, almost twice as many as in 2020. And 88 percent of the satellites launched in the past year were linked to private operators, compared with 23 percent in 2010. Space is no longer just a matter for states and government agencies, it is a rapidly expanding market in which major private companies have taken on an increasingly important role.

However, the picture of launches also shows just how far Europe still lags behind in terms of autonomy. In 2025 there were 181 American orbital launch attempts and 92 Chinese ones, compared with only eight European launches. Yet the continent has an industrial value chain that is anything but marginal: according to Eurospace, it comprises more than 750 companies and institutions and in 2025 recorded almost 11 billion euro in sales.

It is precisely this gap between industrial capacity and strategic autonomy that makes the European question central. The Rome Forum, entitled "The Gate to Sky: Space for Peace", addresses the other side of the competition: who sets the rules, how to ensure the peaceful and sustainable use of space and how to prevent countries with fewer resources from being excluded from the new orbital economy.

Organised by the Italian Space Agency (ASI) and the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), the forum forms part of Italy's presidency of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), which it took over in June for the 2026-2027 biennium. The role gives Rome a prominent position in international space diplomacy.

COPUOS, created in 1959 and made up of 110 member states, is the main multilateral United Nations body for cooperation and the peaceful use of space. Issues on the table include managing satellite traffic, dealing with debris in orbit, access to space technologies and the need to update international rules. These topics no longer concern only space agencies: satellites now underpin essential services for communications, navigation, environmental monitoring and security.

Europe, first-class expertise but autonomy to be strengthened

This is also where Europe's position is measured. The continent has significant scientific and industrial assets, but still needs to turn them into a more autonomous strategic capability. In the new race to the Moon, Washington and Beijing have clearly defined national goals and programmes. Europe takes part in major international initiatives, but does not always manage to present itself as a single actor.

The collaboration with the United States in the Artemis programme is one example: the European Space Agency (ESA) is contributing to the mission with the service module for the Orion capsule, which is crucial for power, propulsion and life support. But the European contribution is not limited to acting as a technological partner.

The Argonaut programme, developed by ESA, aims to secure autonomous access to the lunar surface from the 2030s, with a first lander planned by 2030. The industrial consortium for the descent module will be led by Thales Alenia Space Italia, together with companies from other European countries.

The issue, therefore, is not just reaching the Moon, but having the technologies, launchers and infrastructure needed in order not to be entirely dependent on others. It is also a security challenge: in January 2026 the European External Action Service updated the EU's strategy for security and defence in space, highlighting as priorities the protection of orbital assets, reducing technological dependencies and strengthening Europe's ability to access space autonomously.

The European Union, in short, is not absent from the race. But its role remains divided between ESA's industrial and scientific dimension, EU policies and the initiatives of individual states. Coordination between these levels is precisely what makes the difference, in a field where national investment and decision making risk creating fragmentation rather than a shared strategy.

Italy is banking on space diplomacy

For Italy, the Rome forum is an opportunity to showcase its role in this landscape. The presidency of COPUOS, entrusted to it for 2026-2027, allows the country to contribute directly to the debate on international rules, from the sustainability of activities in orbit to lunar exploration. ASI president Teodoro Valente has been elected to chair the committee.

During the forum, discussions focused on three broad strands: using space technologies to tackle climate change and prevent natural disasters; ensuring fairer access to satellite technologies for emerging countries; and building an international governance framework able to keep pace with the growth of the private sector.

Since the first edition in Trento in 2016, the initiative has involved around 130 countries, with stops in Nairobi, Buenos Aires, Reggio Calabria, Panama, Manama and Manila. In Rome the delegations worked on the "Rome Page", a final declaration intended to gather recommendations and priorities for international cooperation.

Twenty years after her husband's murder in London, one of the most notorious Russian intelligence operations on foreign soil, Marina Litvinenko warns Europe against negotiating with Putin from a position of weakness and says justice requires a trial of his regime in Russia.

The West's failure to respond decisively to the assassination of former Russian intelligence officer Alexander Litvinenko in London in 2006 emboldened Vladimir Putin, paving the way for Russia's war against Ukraine and its threats to wider European security, his widow Marina Litvinenko told Euronews.

Speaking on the 20th anniversary of her husband's death, following the publication of her memoir, A Life in Fragments, Litvinenko described his killing as "the first act of nuclear terrorism in London".

"And what was the reaction? It was not a very serious reaction at all. And what we have now? We have a war in Ukraine," she said.

She warned that Putin continued to test the West's resolve and that further hesitation risked an even wider conflict.

The images that shocked the world

An outspoken Kremlin critic who had served in Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), Alexander Litvinenko fled Russia with his family in 2000 and was granted political asylum in Britain the following year.

From exile, he continued to investigate alleged corruption within Russia's intelligence services and their links to organised crime. He became a British citizen in October 2006, just weeks before his death.

On 23 November, 2006, Litvinenko died at the age of 44 after being poisoned with radioactive polonium-210.

Photographs of Litvinenko lying in a London hospital bed, his head bald and his body ravaged by radiation poisoning, appeared on newspaper front pages around the world. They became an enduring symbol of the dangers faced by Putin's opponents, even in exile.

As his condition deteriorated, his wife refused to give up hope that he would survive.

"I still believe to last moment, Sasha will survive and he will continue to fight against this monster who is the president of Russia still now," Litvinenko recalled.

"And I believed he will survive and we will have a future life, but it did not happen. And I always remember how Sasha was strong to last minute of his life."

The assassination exposed the reach of Russia's intelligence services and foreshadowed further attacks on European soil attributed to Moscow, including the 2018 poisoning of former Russian intelligence officer Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in Salisbury and the 2019 murder of former Chechen separatist commander Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin.

A British public inquiry concluded in 2016 that Litvinenko's murder was carried out by Andrei Lugovoi and Dmitry Kovtun and that the operation was probably approved by both then-FSB chief Nikolai Patrushev and Putin himself.

In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Russia was responsible for Litvinenko's death and had failed to conduct an effective investigation. Moscow has denied responsibility.

Europe's pursuit of 'business as usual' with Putin

"It was not a strong reaction in 2006 because United Kingdom was alone," Marina Litvinenko told Euronews.

Despite the EU's economic strength, she said European governments remained reluctant to jeopardise their relations with Moscow, believing they could continue doing business with Putin.

Now, amid US-led diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine, Western governments are once again debating the terms of engagement with Moscow.

Asked whether the West should negotiate with Putin, Litvinenko said: "Of course you have to negotiate, but not in a way what you allowed Putin to have what he wants. You need to be much stronger and believe in yourself."

She pointed to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as an example for European leaders.

"You can see the Ukrainian president who is very strong in his small country and fighting against this huge country and what everybody believes like a second army in the world," Litvinenko said.

"European Union, it's much bigger and stronger. And you just trust yourself."

Justice must ultimately come from Russia

Neither of the two men identified by the British public inquiry as responsible for Litvinenko's death faced trial in the UK.

While his widow regards the legal proceedings in London and Strasbourg as significant achievements, she believes ultimate accountability must come from within Russia itself.

"But justice only happened after Russia will have their own trial against this regime," she said.

Litvinenko sees the end of the war in Ukraine as a potential turning point, expressing confidence that her husband's case would form a central part of any future prosecution of Putin's government for crimes she attributes to it over the past two decades.

'He would be on the side of Ukraine'

Reflecting on how her husband might view Russia and Europe today, Litvinenko recalled his opposition to Putin's second war in Chechnya and his support for the Chechen independence movement.

She described his support for exiled Chechen leader Akhmed Zakayev, a close friend of the family, as part of his efforts to bring about change in Russia.

It "was a part of his Russian duty to make Russia possible to change", she said.

Twenty years after his murder, Litvinenko has no doubt where her husband would stand today.

"And now I'm 100% sure he would be on the side of Ukraine."

Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO made him about $34 billion (€31bn) richer and added roughly $950 billion (€871bn) to the chipmaker's value in a single day. US President Donald Trump, Nvidia's staff and stock markets from New York to Seoul gained too, while Europe got a smaller lift.

Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday added about $34 billion (€31bn) to his fortune, according to Forbes' real-time billionaires list.

Nvidia's shares closed 31.5% higher, lifting the company's market value by about $950 billion (€871bn), the largest one-day gain for any company on record.

The rally also lifted US President Donald Trump's investments, the wealth of Nvidia's staff and share prices across the US and Asia, while Europe felt a smaller boost.

Trump, who had pushed for Huang's return, told CNBC on Monday that he had "convinced" Nvidia's board. "I made the deal," he boasted.

Nvidia's board received "input from senior levels of the United States government", according to a company statement.

Trump's accounts could have held between 32,000 and 370,000 Nvidia shares as of 30 September, according to a Financial Times analysis of his mandatory financial disclosures. The US president has added to his Nvidia position several times since returning to the White House.

Assuming no recent change in those holdings, the shares would have gained between $1.3 million (€1.2m) and $15 million (€14m) in value on Monday. The filings give only value ranges and do not yet cover October and November.

Trump's portfolio is run independently by third-party financial institutions, according to the White House.

A workforce of millionaires

Employees greeted Huang with cheers, applause and chants of his name when he returned to Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, California, on Monday.

"Thank you all for the second chance," he told them, in footage shared online.

Many have grown rich from the company's rise. In a 2024 poll on Blind, an anonymous forum for verified tech workers, 76% of Nvidia employees who took part said they were millionaires. More than four in ten put their net worth at $10 million (€9.2m) or more.

Share-based pay cost Nvidia $6.4 billion (€5.9bn) in the financial year to January, according to its annual report. Workers can also buy a limited amount of its stock at a discount of at least 15%.

Staff turnover among its roughly 42,000 employees was 3.7% that year, according to the same filing.

Individual holdings are not public, but many staff are likely to still hold much of their wealth in Nvidia shares, which Monday's jump made significantly more valuable.

That gives them reason to see Huang as the man who made them rich and should keep running the company. More than 10,000 people who claimed to work at Nvidia reportedly signed a petition calling for his return.

Stock markets ride the wave

On Wall Street, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5% higher on Monday and the S&P 500 gained 4.7%, their strongest sessions since April 2025.

The S&P 500 won back about $3 trillion (€2.7trn) in market value as the rally also spread to Asia on Tuesday.

Taiwan's Taiex closed 9% higher and South Korea's Kospi rose 6.3%, back above 5,000 points.

Japan's Nikkei 225, which was shut on Monday for a public holiday, gained 3.9%.

On the other hand, Europe's gains were considerably smaller. On Monday, the pan-European Stoxx 600 rose 1.8%, while Germany's DAX added 2.2% and the UK's FTSE 100 about 1.3%.

Chip stocks such as ASML jumped on Monday, but the main European indices were actually slightly down on Tuesday morning.

A key reason for the muted reaction is that Europe's markets hold far fewer tech companies. Technology accounts for 9.5% of the Stoxx 600, according to index provider Stoxx, while banks are its biggest sector at 16.2%.

Huang now faces three House committees behind closed doors on 1 December, then a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on 3 December, a date its chair, Senator Tim Scott, confirmed on Monday.

The technology has been found to be “technically uncertain and very high cost” - yet the European Commission is funding it.

The COP31 climate talks ended without a deal after the EU and others rejected a final deal which failed to mention fossil fuels. But another sticking point was carbon capture and storage - technologies designed to prevent CO2 from entering the atmosphere in the first place and/or to remove it after it has been emitted.

The proposed text backed carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), including a target of at least 500 million tonnes of annual capacity by 2035 and a longer-term ambition of 1.3 billion to 2.5 billion tonnes.

Critics argue that carbon capture without a clear fossil fuel transition risks extending the lifeline of oil and gas. Questions around costs, energy requirements, environmental safeguards and long-term storage liability remain unresolved.

As one of the most divisive topics in climate action, we look into the facts about carbon capture and how the EU came to be funding this experimental technology.

How the European Commission is funding carbon capture and storage

In September this year, the European Commission celebrated their investment in what the owners are calling the “largest commercial carbon capture and storage (CCS) project in Europe”.

CO2 emitted by a fertiliser factory in the Netherlands will be stored underneath the seabed in Norway.

At an opening ceremony this week, the ammonia and fertiliser plant announced that it will capture 800,000 tonnes of CO2 a year then liquefy it to be sent by ship to Norway.

Having funded the project, the European Commission was keen to promote its investment – with the Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth attending the inauguration alongside the Prime Ministers of both countries.

While the Commission says the Sluiskil plant, run by Norwegian chemical company Yara, is a “strategic investment”, opponents say it is “risking billions in taxpayers’ money to fund a dangerous distraction that delays climate action”.

What is carbon capture and storage?

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) refers to technologies designed to prevent CO2 from entering the atmosphere in the first place and/or to remove it after it has been emitted.

As is done at the Sluiskil plant, most projects use a liquid to chemically remove the CO2 emitted from the production process, where it is then compressed into a liquid-like state and transported typically through a pipeline to a storage site. At that point, it’s either stored deep underground or is transformed into things like building materials or synthetic fuel. In the case of the latter, this technology is referred to as CCUS, where the ‘U’ stands for utilisation.

As of February 2026, there were 75 operational CCS projects around the world, according to climate change publication Carbon Brief. Almost all of them are at fossil-fuel extraction and processing sites, according to the IEA’s database. Together, these projects capture 62.5 million tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2) each year. This is equivalent to 0.2 per cent of total global emissions in 2025.

While Yara’s chief executive, Svein Tore Holsether, said in a statement, “The carbon capture facility in Sluiskil proves that large-scale industrial decarbonisation is possible today”, the cumulative emissions saved are a very, very tiny drop in the ocean.

US non-profit the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) has conducted in-depth research into CCS. Their Energy Finance Analyst, Andrew Reid, says: “Despite the political and financial support that has been pointed to CCS over the past three to four years, it remains technically uncertain, very high cost, and reliant upon huge subsidies to move from feasibility to construction and operation.”

CCS: To help the fossil fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas

To understand its uses, it’s important to understand where carbon technology originates from. According to Carbon Brief, it “was originally rolled out at US and Canadian oil wells in the early 1970s as a way to achieve “enhanced oil recovery”. This involves injecting captured CO2 into depleted wells – a process that stores the gas, but also helps to extract more oil.” This is by far the most significant use for carbon capture worldwide, with three-quarters of it used for this purpose.

This means that “the majority of CO2 that is both captured and used today helps the fossil-fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas,” according to Carbon Brief.

How did the EU end up funding carbon capture and storage?

One of the arguments against CCS, which campaigners have been making for years, is that it is a way for polluters to keep polluting, rather than emitting less of the gases which are heating up the planet at alarming rates.

“All capture and storage projects suffer from the same problem: they distract attention and resources from cutting emissions at source and give polluting industries like fertiliser production a pass to keep on polluting,” says Rachel Kennerley, Senior International Carbon Capture Campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL). 

Belén Balanyá, researcher and campaigner at Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO), has been tracking the lobbying efforts of the fossil fuel industry for 25 years. She has recently focussed on lobbying by the CCS industry. The outcomes of annual COP climate talks are known to be influenced by lobbyists representing industry. Balanyá found that around 500 CCS lobbyists were at COP29 in 2024. A year earlier, at COP28, CCS proponents (largely tied to fossil fuel industries) scored a significant win with the endorsement of “abatement and removal technologies” in the agreement.

Referring to fossil fuel industries, Balanyá says, “You look at what’s on the agenda and it’s always escape hatches to stay in business,” she tells Euronews Green. “It’s where they move when they’ve been forced to – when there’s more knowledge and more acceptance about climate change and their role and that they have to decarbonise.”

CCS being endorsed in a COP agreement may have contributed to its legitimacy in political circles within the EU. The CCUS Forum (now the Industrial Carbon Management (ICM) Forum), set up by the European Commission in 2021, is an annual event with working groups that feed directly into EU policymaking. CEO found that every group has been co-chaired by the fossil fuel industry or associated organisations.

A newly released report from the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) details the risks of overshooting 1.5°C of warming and how we can limit them. It assessed what it called Carbon Dioxide Removal and found that many issues remain with the technology, such as whether it can scale sustainably (due to costs, land and energy use), whether it would actually keep CO2 out of the atmosphere permanently and who’s responsible for regulation and leaks.

CCS: Good or bad?

Wherever commentators stand on CCS, there is some agreement that for some industries, the technology can be useful. Yara’s project targets emissions from ammonia production which “provides a relatively concentrated CO2 stream, making this one of the more straightforward industrial applications of carbon capture rather than an example of the very hardest emissions to abate,” according to Domien Vangenechten, Programme Lead in Clean Economy at E3G.

“The lesson should therefore not be that Europe needs CCS everywhere, but that we should pragmatically deploy it where it can cut substantial emissions today.”

The reform plans come as Brussels tries to preserve multilateral climate diplomacy while relying on smaller coalitions of countries willing to move ahead on key issues like the phasing out of fossil fuels.

The European Commission is drawing up plans to overhaul the UN climate summit process, warning that the current negotiating system risks becoming ineffective because a single country can block an agreement among nearly 200 parties.

The push follows the chaotic COP31 climate conference, which ended without consensus on a political declaration reaffirming the commitment to transition away from fossil fuels agreed at COP28 in Dubai.

Brussels says the failure has exposed deeper flaws in the process, from a lack of transparency and cumbersome decision-making to the inability of the annual climate summits to translate existing commitments into action.

“If we want to save the COP, it needs to reform itself,” a senior Commission official said on Tuesday during a briefing following the negotiations.

The Commission will draw up its reform proposals in consultation with EU member states.

Brussels wants to ensure that work outside the formal negotiations – through coalitions of willing countries – continues to advance the climate transition that governments have so far struggled to deliver through consensus.

Despite the COP31 fiasco, several EU countries, like Finland, Denmark, Portugal and Spain, have unveiled their own roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels.

Overhauling the COP system

The EU says there needs to be more transparency about how negotiations are conducted, when proposals are introduced and why positions change.

"The minister from Ghana objected to the very significant lack of transparency and democratic process in the COP. So we are far from alone in saying this. Preparing for the next COP means that we have to immediately draw the lessons from what happened," the senior Commission official added.

The lack of visibility over the decision-making process also became a source of frustration during COP31, with Brussels saying its plans will try to overcome negotiating deadlocks.

Under the current consensus-based system, a single country can prevent an agreement from being adopted, even when a large majority of parties support it.

Brussels wants to explore ways to address this problem while preserving the democratic legitimacy of the multilateral process.

The Commission is also concerned that countries are repeatedly reopening political agreements instead of delivering on them, particularly the COP28 commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, which was later endorsed by the UN summit in Santa Marta, Colombia.

The Commission says the EU and a coalition of more than 130 countries sought to reaffirm the Dubai agreement, including its commitments to triple renewable energy capacity, double energy efficiency improvements and transition away from fossil fuels.

But negotiations broke down over resistance from a group led by Saudi Arabia, which Brussels accused of seeking to replace the fossil fuel transition language with a greater emphasis on carbon capture and storage.

The proposed text included a target for carbon capture on a gigaton scale by 2035, which the EU considered "unacceptable" because it risked allowing continued fossil fuel use.

"That is simply impossible to achieve and impossible to accept, because this would have given a lifeline to the continuation of fossil energy in the energy system," the senior Commission official argued.

The Commission estimates that between 80 and 90 countries objected to the final proposed political declaration, including all 27 EU member states, the UK, Norway and Switzerland, as well as more than 40 least developed countries.

Japan, Canada and Egypt also supported the objections politically, according to the EU's assessment.

Brussels rejects COP31's total failure

Brussels insisted the failure to agree on the declaration does not mean the entire summit was unsuccessful.

The senior Commission official cited decisions on other parts of the climate agenda, including carbon markets and the $103 billion pledged by development banks for climate finance, as positive steps forward.

However, the breakdown has intensified questions about whether the UN process can maintain political momentum on climate action when countries remain deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels.

The Commission also wants to streamline the expanding range of issues discussed at climate summits.

An increasing number of working groups and parallel initiatives are diverting attention from the core task of reducing emissions and implementing the Paris Agreement, the senior Commission official said.

Trade measures have consumed significant negotiating energy despite not being central to the original purpose of the COP process, the Commission noted.

Nonetheless, budget pressures are likely to fuel the debate over whether the COP still makes sense, with the United States' withdrawal expected to have financial implications for the organisation and its operations.

It's worth going outside to enjoy the Moon tonight - it will look bigger and brighter than usual.

We’ll be treated to a Supermoon tonight - and it’s set to be big and bright.

The night of 23rd to 24th November will see the Beaver Supermoon light up the sky.

November’s full Moon is traditionally known as the 'Beaver Moon', a nickname linked to the time of year when beavers prepare for winter by building dams and gathering food.

What is a Supermoon?

The November 2026 full Moon is a Supermoon, which means it occurs when the Moon is at or near its closest point to Earth. That is possible because its orbit isn't a perfect circle. Instead, it's elliptical, or slightly egg-shaped.

That means the distance between the two bodies varies. When the Moon is at its closest point to Earth, it's at perigee. When the Moon is furthest from Earth, it's at apogee.

The technical name for a Supermoon is a perigee full Moon, and it can appear up to 14 per cent larger and 30 per cent brighter than a full Moon at apogee.

How to watch a Supermoon - and the best time to see it

A Supermoon can be seen in clear night skies without any special equipment.

Try to find a wide, open space, preferably one that's elevated, such as up a hill.

It's such an exciting spectacle because, whether a Supermoon or not, the Moon appears bigger when it's close to the horizon because of what's called the 'Moon illusion'. This is a strange visual trick that experts can't yet fully explain. "When you have a supermoon, that effect is just slightly more striking,” said astronomer William Alston with the University of Hertfordshire in the United Kingdom.

The best time to view a Supermoon

Experts say the best times to view a Supermoon are at moonrise and moonset, when the Moon is close to the horizon.

For most of western Europe, moonrise will be between 4 and 5pm today.

You can check exact moonrise times for where you live here.

If you miss moonrise, don't worry. The Supermoon will still be impressive throughout the night and into tomorrow as well (25th November).

When is the next Supermoon?

An anomalistic month (from one perigee to the next) is shorter than a synodic month (from one New Moon to the next) - but only by around two days. This means that if a full Moon falls close to perigee in one month, it is likely to do so again the following month.

The consequence of this is that, when Supermoons happen, they happen in groups - we get four or five Super Full Moons in a row (or four or five Super New Moons in a row).

Tonight’s will be the second to last Supermoon of the year. The last Supermoon of 2026 could be particularly magical, as it will rise on 24th December, celebrated as Christmas Eve in many European countries.

The next two Supermoons after that will be on 22nd January 2027 and 20th February 2027.

How do Supermoons affect tides?

The tides are caused by the gravitational forces of the Sun and the Moon on the Earth’s oceans, explains Royal Museums Greenwich. When the Moon is closer to the Earth during a Supermoon, the gravitational pull is slightly stronger, and so the tides are bigger. However this effect is almost negligible, with only a few centimetres difference between a normal full Moon and Supermoon tide.

However, full Moon and New Moon tides can be much bigger than those at other times in the lunar month, as the Sun adds its own gravitational pull into the mix, producing the so-called spring tides.

The Beaver Supermoon is set to have potentially damaging effects along the west coast of the US, for example. High tides along the Pacific Coast could break 40-year-old records and flood low-lying coastal communities, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week.

In the San Francisco Bay Area, tides could reach almost a metre above normal on Tuesday before peaking on Wednesday, says Dial Hoang, a National Weather Service forecaster.

Reporterii Info Sud-Est, Átlátszó Erdély, Monitorul de Botoșani și Context.ro au inventariat principalele cauze pentru care România a pierdut miliarde de euro din Programul Național de Redresare și Reziliență (PNRR). Am adunat date de la guvern, de la autorități locale și de la mediul de afaceri, iar poza de final, conform acestor surse, arată că programul a fost scris fără priorități clare, lipsit de transparență, de multe ori a fost supracontractat și că multe proiecte incluse în listă erau utopice pentru că, previzibil, urmau să fie blocate în birocrație.

Într-un răspuns oficial transmis la finalul lunii septembrie, Guvernul, prin Ministerul Investițiilor și Proiectelor Europene (MIPE) condus la acea vreme de Dragoș Pîslaru, a recunoscut că PNRR a întâmpinat probleme majore încă din primele luni. Planul a cărui paternitate și-a arogat-o fostul ministru USR, Cristian Ghinea, a fost construit „fără criterii transparente și obiective de selecție” și fără o listă de priorități. 

Potrivit funcționarilor de la MIPE, planul lui Ghinea, aprobat de Comisia Europeană,  nu prevedea un sistem de prioritizare a investiţiilor care să ţină cont de factori precum maturitatea lor tehnică, capacitatea reală de execuţie, impactul şi riscul de nefinalizare al acestora . Ministerul susține că lipsa acestor criterii a dus la supracontractare, adică la asumarea unor angajamente financiare peste resursele disponibile, și la eliminarea ulterioară a unor proiecte care ar fi putut fi excluse încă de la început.

Sursa foto: răspunsul Ministerului Investiţiilor şi Proiectelor Europene

În ceea ce privește implementarea, potrivit MIPE, principalele obstacole semnalate de “coordonatorii de reforme și/sau investiții” şi de beneficiarii proiectelor au fost: 

  • capacitatea administrativă redusă: deficitul de personal specializat raportat la profilul şi complexitatea investițiilor, 
  • durata procedurilor de achiziții, raportată la timpul limitat pentru implementarea PNRR, 
  • întârzierile în procesarea cererilor de transfer,
  • problemele de coordonare şi comunicare între autorităţile centrale şi locale,
  • întârzierile în obținerea avizelor necesare şi
  • angajamentul politic insuficient.

Context.ro i-a cerut lui Cristian Ghinea, ministrul responsabil pentru realizarea și negocierea planului în forma sa inițială, un punct de vedere asupra acestor aspecte, dar nu am primit un răspuns până la acest moment.

MIPE a atras atenția că programele precum PNRR trebuie să fie transparente și supuse controlului civic.

“În același timp, transparența trebuie să fie o componentă esențială a acestei arhitecturi. Cetățenii și societatea civilă, în general, trebuie să aibă acces simplu, rapid și inteligibil la informațiile de interes public, inclusiv prin platforme și instrumente digitale care să permită urmărirea proiectelor, investițiilor, reformelor, a finanțărilor în general și a rezultatelor acestora.”

Numeroase investigații au evidențiat lipsa de transparență a programului, inclusiv la nivelul Comisiei Europene. Inclusiv Curtea de Conturi a UE a subliniat că lipsa transparenței privind modul în care au fost cheltuiți banii a reprezentat o problemă majoră. 

Bani pierduți pentru că “s-au greșit documentațiile pentru autorizația de construcție”

Am încercat să aflăm de la funcționari publici și de la un reprezentant al companiilor din domeniul construcțiilor care au fost problemele cele mai grave cu PNRR pe care le-au observat ei. 

Raluca-Ştefania Curelariu, fosta prefectă judeţului Botoşani, numită cu susţinerea USR, a explicat că județul ei a avut proiecte 224 de milioane de euro și că unele au mers prost pentru că, în unele cazuri “autoritățile au gresit din start proiectele”, sau proiectele au avut o “proastă planificare”:

“Ne-am trezit cu o lună înainte: «Stai că eu n-am racordul la utilități!». Pe ultima sută de metri ne-am trezit că avem foarte multe proiecte pe care nu le putem închide, pentru că nu fuseseră făcute demersurile din timp pentru racordare. Asta este o chestiune de planificare, din punctul meu de vedere, care ar fi putut fi gestionată mult, mult mai bine”, a povestit fosta prefectă a județului Botoșani. 

Raluca-Ştefania Curelariu a mai explicat că, în cazul unui centru pentru copii în risc de abandon, finanțat parțial din PNRR, proiectul n-a fost trecut ca finalizat pentru că “autorizația de construire fusese dată în condiții suspecte”.

“Noi, ca Instituția Prefectului, în momentul în care am fost sesizați în urma unui control al celor de la Inspectoratul de Stat în Construcții, am fost obligați să mergem în instanță, să cerem anularea autorizației. Neavând autorizație valabilă, bineînțeles că nu se poate face recepția.”, a explicat Raluca-Ştefania Curelariu. Ea a mai adăugat că alte patru proiecte au pierdut finantarea europeană pentru că “s-au greșit documentațiile pentru autorizația de construcție.”

Peste aceste incidente legale s-a suprapus uneori și lipsa de seriozitate a constructorilor care, deși aveau termene contractuale ferme, nu le-au respectat, a explicat reprezentanta guvernului în Botoșani.

Constructorii acuză: trei ani și jumătate pentru birocrație și doar un an și jumătate pentru muncă

De cealaltă parte, un reprezentant al constructorilor spune că PNRR avea termene de implementare nerealiste. “Nu este posibil ca într-un program de 5 ani, 3,5 ani să fie consumați pentru definirea proiectului, din păcate, nu după niște rigori de prioritizare care să fie posibil de realizat și în timpul care a mai rămas de circa 1,5 ani constructorul, care este ultima verigă în acest lanț investițional, să trebuiască să execute lucrările”, a povestit Adriana Iftime, directoarea generală a Federației Patronatelor Societăților din Construcții. 

Reprezentanța constructorilor a explicat că în 2026 antreprenorii au făcut un efort substanțial ca să termine până la 31 august lucrările în așa fel încât ele să poată intra la decontările către Comisia Europeană.

“Constructorii au trebuit să se mobilizeze, să abandoneze proiecte care erau importante pentru ei, dar nu reprezentau interesul PNRR-ului, și să gestioneze, într-un mod cât de cât acceptabil, problema crizei de forță de muncă. A fost adusă forță de muncă din străinătate, din Asia, acolo este sursa noastră de forță de muncă.”, a explicat directoarea patronatelor din construcții.

PNRR, umflat electoral

Însă acest efort a venit și cu o doză de risc, spune Adriana Iftime, pentru că plățile de la stat către contractori sunt lente și sunt îngreunate de birocrați. “Asta înseamnă că în zona noastră au fost inițial cca nouă miliarde de euro; am realizat investiții de circa șase miliarde, dar la 31 august erau achitate, plătite doar jumătate, circa trei miliarde. Pentru guvernanți este liniștitor faptul că ei vor spune întotdeauna nu e nici un fel de problemă aceste datorii se vor achita, da, suntem convinși că se vor achita, dar pentru un constructor este foarte important momentul în care se va achita. Pentru că, dacă el nu va putea participa la alte licitații, nu va putea să-și asigure investițiile pe următorul an, constructorii gândesc: în următorul an, în următorii ani, ei își asigură firma cu contracte ca să-și facă niște socoteli”, a explicat Iftime. 

Una dintre problemele identificate de repezentanta constructorilor a fost că guvernul a permis supracontractarea PNRR-ului – adică mai multe proiecte decât banii disponibili. Iftime spune că aceasta este o metodă veche utilizată de autorități pentru a crește volumul de bani europeni pe care i-am consumat. În cazul PNRR, metoda n-a avut succes.

 “De data aceasta, supracontractarea a fost mult mai mare, a depășit niște limite gestionabile, nu s-au supracontractat proiectele mature, proiectele care aveau și perspectiva de a fi finalizate. Mi-aș permite un comentariu așa, puțin în paranteză: probabil că supracontractarea asta a fost influențată de interese electorale, de interese politice. De asta vă spuneam la început, interesul politic și electoral este prea dominant în raport cu ceea ce poate să facă piața.”

Cazul microbuzelor electrice fără stații de încărcare

Otilia Moruz, directorul Direcției de Dezvoltare și Promovare din cadrul Consiliului Județean (CJ) Botoșani, spune că multe proiecte de mediu au fost abandonate pentru că din start n-a existat o planificare care să țină cont de birocrația existentă. “Tot ce ține de mediu vizează proceduri de lungă durată. Și, iarăși, statul, prin autoritățile pe care le gestionează, știe foarte clar cât durează obținerea unui aviz de mediu sau a unui studiu de impact asupra mediului. Numai elaborarea lui durează două-trei luni. Apoi avizarea, apoi consultări publice. Deci e un proces, să zic, de minim șase luni pentru un proiect care impactează mediul. Deci, automat, trebuia să se aibă în vedere toate aceste etape care trebuiesc parcurse.”

Reprezentanta Consiliului Județean oferă un exemplu concret de proiect ratat, cel al microbuzelor școlare electrice, unde “la centru” nu s-a luat în calcul că în zonele rurale nu există stații de încărcare.

“Și vă dau un exemplu: ghidul de finanțare pentru microbuze electrice a vizat strict zone defavorizate ale județelor, unde, în mod cert, nu sunt stații de încărcare electrică, da? Deci, din start, cumva, a fost grea implementarea, pentru că fiecare UAT a trebuit să își asume că obține de la Delgaz ATR-uri, că asigură instalarea și montarea cel puțin a unei stații de încărcare electrică pentru microbuz… adică au fost tot soiul de etape care puteau cumva fi evitate prin construcția ghidului de finanțare”, a declarat Otilia Moruz.

Niciunul dintre miniștri Fondurilor Europene în perioada negocierii și derulării PNRR – Cristian Ghinea, Marcel Boloș, Florin Cîțu, Dan Vîlceanu, Adrian Câciu și Dragoș Pîslaru – nu au răspuns solicitării unui punct de vedere referitor la eșecul celor peste 1600 de proiecte eliminate din PNRR.

În noiembrie, Piano Express a revenit pe străzile Bucureștiului, invitând trecătorii la întâlniri incognito cu muzica contemporană și cu povești despre cartierele orașului. Ajuns la a patra ediție, proiectul inițiat de pianista Adriana Toacsen a explorat, sub tema Amintiri Noi, felul în care arhitectura și amintirile personale se întâlnesc în locurile pe care le traversăm zilnic. Componenta de arhitectură a fost curatoriată de Dorothée Hasnaș, care a conturat traseele urbane și poveștile locurilor cărora Adriana le-a răspuns prin muzică.

Programul a cuprins două concerte gratuite, patru tururi urbane ghidate de Teodor Frolu, Florin Cristescu, Ilinca Păun Constantinescu și Robert Zotescu, un silent concert în cadrul ultimului tur ghidat și întâlniri muzicale cu elevii Liceului de Arte Plastice „Nicolae Tonitza” și ai Școlii Aletheea. Un apel public – deschis în continuare – i-a invitat pe bucureșteni să contribuie cu propriile fotografii și povești la memoria orașului.

În cei patru ani, pianul a străbătut Bucureștiul dintr-un cartier în altul, ieșind din sălile de concert și poposind în grădini, curți interioare și spații publice. A fost în Parcul Ioanid și Vatra Luminoasă, în Berceni și Drumul Taberei, dar și în locuri încărcate de istorie, precum Parcul Izvor, Biserica Kretzulescu sau Muzeul Țăranului Român. Anul trecut, traseul a urmărit arhitectura modernistă, cu opriri la Biblioteca Academiei Române, Facultatea de Drept și campusul Politehnicii. În jurul pianului, s-au adunat peste cinzeci de muzicieni, alături de ansambluri de muzică contemporană și jazz, Corul de Cameră „Preludiu”, sau compozitori, arhitecți și istorici. Pianistă și profesoară la Universitatea Națională de Muzică din București, Adriana Toacsen are o coardă sensibilă pentru muzica contemporană, în jurul căreia dezvoltă proiecte culturale, din dorința de a promova creații românești și de a-i găsi ascultători noi.

Am stat de vorbă cu Adriana Toacsen despre ce lasă în urmă un pian plimbat prin București, cum alege muzica în dialog cu arhitectura locurilor și cum ne invită aceste întâlniri să redescoperim orașul cu alți ochi. Și, mai ales, cu alte urechi.

Povesteai într-un interviu că Piano Express a apărut ca idee într-o seară în Timișoara, când, după un concert, te plimbai prin Piața Libertății și ai întâlnit un necunoscut care cânta la un pian instalat în stradă. Te-ai așezat pe o bancă să-l asculți și de acolo a pornit gândul de a aduce un pian și pe străzile Bucureștiului. Ce te-a impresionat atât de mult la întâlnirea aceea? Și ce a rămas din acel gând până azi?

Mi-am dorit ca pianul să-ți iasă în cale, să-l punem în locuri în care să te împiedici de el. Și asta încercăm să facem de fiecare dată, să alegem locuri în care oamenii nu s-ar aștepta neapărat să găsească un pian. Sigur, uneori ne îndreptăm spre un loc anume pentru povestea lui, ca anul trecut în campusul Politehnicii – ne-a atras arhitectura lui modernistă, așa că am organizat acolo un concert de pian și pian de jucărie, urmat de un tur ghidat prin campus. Îmi place foarte mult ideea că nu trebuie neapărat să vii tu după muzică, ci vine ea spre tine,  te întâlnești cu ea pur și simplu, într-o zi obișnuită, când ai cu totul altceva de făcut.

E minunat și când oamenii vin special pentru un concert. Spre bucuria noastră, avem deja un public care ne „urmărește” prin oraș. Ni s-a întâmplat încă din primul an. Am cunoscut o familie cărora le-a plăcut atât de mult al doilea concert, încât au hotărât să vină la toate celelalte. Mi se pare extraordinar când cineva descoperă ceva ce-i place și vrea să meargă mai departe cu noi.

Îmi doresc la fel de mult și întâlnirile întâmplătoare. Să treacă cineva pe stradă, să vadă pianul și să spună: „Ia uite, ce-i aici?”.... și să se oprească. Poate rămâne cinci minute, poate o jumătate de oră. Nu trebuie să asculte un concert întreg ca să se întâmple ceva. Poate aude o piesă care-i place, află numele unui compozitor despre care nu știa nimic și, peste câteva luni, îl recunoaște într-un program de concert, poate descoperă un loc din oraș pe lângă care a trecut de o sută de ori fără să-l privească vreodată cu atenție.

Cred că asta e una dintre mizele proiectului: să facem posibile niște întâlniri care altfel, poate, nu s-ar fi întâmplat. Între oameni și muzică, între oameni și orașul lor. Vrem să arătăm că muzica, inclusiv cea contemporană, nu e ceva de care trebuie să te apropii cu teamă sau pentru care trebuie să ai o pregătire specială. Poți pur și simplu să asculți, să fii curios, să descoperi dacă-ți place. Mi se pare că ar trebui să ne întrebăm mai des, noi, cei care lucrăm în cultură, cum facem să ajungem și în calea celor care nu au, în mod obișnuit, un drum spre noi.

Ediția de anul acesta s-a numit „Amintiri Noi”. Cum ai ajuns la tema asta și ce v-ați dorit să explorați prin muzică?

Anul acesta, Primăria de Verde, de pe Banu Manta, împlinește o sută de ani și am început să ne gândim ce alte foste primării mai știm. Așa am ajuns la cea din Piața Amzei, fosta Primărie de Galben, cunoscută astăzi și prin proiectul deGalben. Eu îmi aminteam clădirea din perioada în care mergeam acolo să plătesc taxe și să depun formulare. Mi se părea un spațiu extraordinar și mă gândeam încă de atunci ce frumos ar fi să fac un concert înăuntru. Apoi mi-am amintit că acolo a funcționat și o casă de căsătorii. O verișoară de-ale mele s-a căsătorit acolo. Pentru că  locuiam în cartier vedeam deseori pe trepte cupluri, oameni cu flori, orez aruncat. Eram martoră la bucuriile lor.

Și de aici a venit ideea cu „Amintiri Noi”. Locurile au deja poveștile și amintirile lor, dar mi se pare frumos să putem adăuga unele noi. Să le oferim oamenilor ocazia să descopere altfel aceste spații și să trăiască acolo ceva ce poate vor ține minte. Poate cineva își va aminti peste ani că într-o fostă primărie a ascultat pentru prima dată o anumită muzică.

Cum alegi muzica pentru locurile în care ajunge Piano Express? Ce a inspirat, de exemplu, programul din Grivița?

Mai întâi încercăm să înțelegem locul, arhitectura și istoria lui, și apoi să găsim legăturile cu muzica. În Grivița, am pornit de la prezența Radiodifuziunii, în jurul căreia au trăit și au lucrat mulți muzicieni. Sala principală de concerte poartă numele lui Mihail Jora, unul dintre cei care au pus bazele școlii românești de compoziție, așa că am inclus în program și câteva lucrări de-ale lui.

Banatul și lecția regiunilor gastronomice europene. Țușpais, hencleș și ciorbe locale, în meniuri degustate de toată Europa

Țușpaisul este o garnitură de legume, servită alături de ouă, de cartofi noi fripți, de pui fript sau de chiftele. Legumele se schimbă după anotimp. Vara se face din ludăiță (dovlecel) sau din călărabă (gulie), primăvara devreme din spanac și mazăre, iar iarna din morcovi.

Premieră în istoria omenirii: sonda Voyager 1 trece de pragul unei zile-lumină și duce cu ea un mesaj care ar putea rezista un miliard de ani

Miercuri, 18 noiembrie, Voyager 1, sonda lansată de NASA în 1977, ajunge la o zi-lumină de Pământ, devenind astfel primul obiect construit de om care parcurge această distanță. Cel mai apropiat obiect de Pământ, Luna, se află la doar 1,3 secunde-lumină.

Jora a fost și profesorul mai multor generații de compozitori și ne-am dorit să ducem povestea mai departe, până în prezent. Așa i-am invitat pe Oana Vardianu și Vlad Ciocoiu să scrie lucrări noi pentru pian. Mi se pare frumos că putem aduce împreună muzica unor generații diferite și, în același timp, să spunem ceva despre locul în care ne aflăm. Încercăm de fiecare dată să facem în așa fel încât povestea orașului și muzica să se completeze. 

Cum se întâlnesc muzica cu arhitectura? Tu ai venit cu muzica, Dorothee cu poveștile locurilor. Cum s-a construit dialogul între voi?

Poate că arhitectura și muzica par arte diferite, dar se pot pune una pe alta în discuție. De exemplu, la Primăria de Verde, turul ghidat a fost însoțit de înregistrări făcute de mine cu lucrări ale unor compozitori născuți în urmă cu  o sută de ani, odată cu clădirea. Mi se pare grozav când artele își unesc forțele și reușesc să creeze împreună o experiență pentru public.

Mi-am dorit să duc pianul și în școli, să le ofer copiilor ocazia să vadă un pianist cântând chiar în fața lor, să poată întreba orice le trece prin cap. La Liceul Tonitza mi s-a părut cu atât mai interesant, pentru că aveam în față copii care sunt, la rândul lor, creatori. Le-am pregătit inclusiv o suită de Carmen Petra-Basacopol, inspirată de trei tablouri, și s-au născut tot felul de discuții, despre cum se întâlnesc muzica și artele vizuale.

Muzica contemporană poate să pară intimidantă. Cum îi faci loc publicului mai puțin obișnuit cu ea?

Cred că e important să apropiem oamenii și de compozitori. La concertul de anul acesta i-am invitat pe aceștia să vorbească și am încurajat publicul să le pună întrebări. N-a fost chiar ușor. Există teama  că ”aș putea să pun o întrebare nepotrivită sau greșită”.  poți să întrebi orice, nu neapărat ceva despre compoziție. Mi se pare important să descoperi omul din spatele muzicii, să vezi că e cineva ca tine, doar că lucrează într-un alt domeniu.

Felul în care construiești un concert poate să ajute, de asemenea. Am făcut la un moment dat un proiect, Encore, pentru care am invitat compozitori să scrie bisuri, piese scurte pentru pian. Bisul mi se pare că are ceva din esența plăcerii muzicale, e un dar pe care îl primești la finalul unui concert.  La concertele Encore, între piese povesteam câte puțin despre compozitori, despre muzica lor și, uneori, despre experiența mea cu lucrarea respectivă. Cred că poți să vorbești despre muzică foarte firesc, fără să pierzi din rigoare. 

Cum e, pentru tine, să cânți în locuri publice, printre zgomotele Bucureștiului, față de o sală de concert? 

E cu mult mai greu să te concentrezi. Afară intervine tot timpul ceva: o mașină, o pasăre, un țânțar, o ambulanță. În sala de concert, spațiul e gândit în așa fel încât să te protejeze de zgomotele din jur. Pe stradă, auzi tot și trebuie să te concentrezi de o sută de ori mai puternic. E mai dificil ca interpret, dar apropierea  de public mi se pare extraordinară.

Tocmai asta ne-am dorit, să ieșim din spațiul convențional al concertului și să fim mai aproape de oameni,  mai aproape de familiile cu copii, pentru că aceasta a fost una dintre dorințele noastre de la început. În multe săli există limite de vârstă și, chiar dacă poți veni cu un copil este posibil ca la un moment dat acesta să nu mai aibă răbdare să stea până la finalul concertului. Atunci, dacă nu ai avut noroc când ai rezervat biletele, trebuie să ridici jumătate de rând ca să ieși. Deranjezi pe toată lumea. Afară e mult mai simplu. Poți să stai cât vrei, să pleci când simți că e momentul. Îmi place foarte mult că dispare distanța dintre scenă și public.

Pentru cel care ascultă, pianul poate avea și efectul invers: are o anumită rezonanță și e impunător, astfel că elimină din zgomotul din jur.

Mie îmi place să spun că te fură. Și eu pățesc asta când sunt în public. Uneori ascult muzica, dar gândurile continuă să mă asalteze, nu reușesc să mă desprind de ele. Alteori mă trezesc că a trecut o vreme și nici nu mi-am dat seama că nu m-am mai gândit la nimic din toate astea. Muzica m-a furat, pur și simplu.

De ce crezi că Bucureștiul are nevoie de astfel de întâlniri neașteptate? Cum poate Piano Express să aducă ceva nou în felul în care ne privim orașul?

Bucureștiul e un oraș foarte grăbit și nu cred că spun ceva nou. Alergăm cu mașina, cu bicicleta, cu trotineta, pe jos și nu prea ridicăm privirea. A început să mă preocupe relația locuitorilor cu orașul lor acum zece ani, când lucram la un proiect numit Muzica Orașului. Mi-am dat seama că și eu eram printre oamenii care aleargă pe trotuar fără să se privească în sus. Am început să privesc mai atent clădirile, să descopăr detalii pe lângă care trecusem de sute de ori. Poți să-ți faci singur un fel de educație a privirii. O clădire frumoasă, dacă te uiți cu adevărat la ea, începe să ți se arate. Tururile ghidate te ajută să faci un pas mai departe, să intri în locuri în care poate altfel n-ai avea acces, să afli poveștile oamenilor care le-au construit sau care au trăit acolo.

Cred că are legătură și cu felul în care ne raportăm la București. Pentru turul din Grivița am făcut o invitație care începea cu două cuvinte: „Orașul tău”. Auzim foarte des că Bucureștiul e murdar, aglomerat, că se construiește prost, că dispar clădiri sau detalii arhitecturale. Sunt probleme reale, nu spun să ne prefacem că totul e frumos. Dar e orașul tău, al meu, al nostru. Mi se pare că, dacă rămâi doar în nemulțumire, nu mai ajungi să vezi și lucrurile pentru care merită să-l iubești.

Asta încercăm să facem și cu Piano Express. Să le dăm oamenilor un motiv să se oprească puțin din alergătura zilnică, să asculte muzică și să descopere orașul în care trăiesc. Poate ajungi pentru un concert și pleci de acolo cu o poveste despre un cartier sau despre o clădire pe lângă care ai trecut de atâtea ori fără să știi nimic despre ea. Mi-ar plăcea ca astfel de întâlniri să ne facă mai curioși, poate și să ne apropie puțin mai mult de București, pentru că, până la urmă, ca să-ți fie drag un oraș, trebuie să ajungi să-l cunoști.

Dacă Bucureștiul ar fi un instrument muzical, care ar fi? Și cum ar suna?

PIANUL. Asta nu doar pentru că sunt pianistă! Bucureștiul e un oraș mare, iar pianul e un instrument cu o dimensiune pe măsură! Are o formă ușor ondulată, iar în interior corzile se încrucișează, se suprapun. Mi se pare o metaforă destul de bună pentru București.

Ca sonoritate, cred că ar fi o muzică contemporană, pentru că e un oraș extrem de divers și de efervescent. Noi îl facem așa, cu cât suntem mai mulți și mai diferiți, cu atât se întâmplă mai multe evenimente. De altfel, ăsta era unul dintre argumentele care mă speriau când mă gândeam să plec din București: că aș rata o mie de momente culturale care se întâmplă în același timp. Îmi place foarte mult energia asta a orașului, în ciuda faptului că uneori poate deveni copleșitoare.

După patru ediții Piano Express, ce ai aflat nou, ce-ți dă energia să-l continui? Și cât de greu e să susții un astfel de proiect cultural, mai ales când finanțările sunt atât de imprevizibile?

În primul rând, mă inspiră reacțiile oamenilor. Ale publicului, dar și ale profesioniștilor pe care îi atragi încet lângă tine. 

Sigur că un astfel de proiect nu e simplu. Anul acesta am pornit destul de greu și a trebuit să reorganizăm multe detalii din mers. Când finanțările se clarifică târziu, tot calendarul se dă peste cap. Oamenii cu care ai stabilit să lucrezi au deja alte angajamente pentru că vorbești despre alte date, cauți soluții diferite și încerci să faci toate astea fără ca publicul să simtă dificultățile din culise. Mi-aș dori să existe mai multă predictibilitate, pentru că energia asta ar putea merge către ceea ce facem.

Ne-a ajutat mult experiența celor patru ediții și faptul că avem deja oameni pe care ne putem baza. Proiectele aduc împreună profesioniști din diverse domenii, care colaborează și își împărtășesc experiențele, descoperind noi perspective asupra propriilor preocupări. Dincolo de bucuria de a oferi publicului experiențe inedite, astfel de întâlniri deschid noi universuri chiar și pentru cei implicați, generând uneori idei neașteptate și facilitând contexte de învățare și inspirație reciprocă.

Piano Express. Amintiri Noi este organizat de Asociația Encore și finanțat de Primăria Sectorului 1, prin programul de finanțare nerambursabilă pentru proiecte culturale.

Security is tight after a recent drone strike near Mukachevo, as Budapest names Russia as the aggressor but rules out sending weapons or troops.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar is holding talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in western Ukraine, where he will also meet leaders of the region's ethnic Hungarian community.

Magyar announced on Facebook that Foreign Minister Anita Orbán would go with him to Zakarpattia, a Ukrainian region bordering Hungary that is home to a sizeable Hungarian minority.

According to preliminary information obtained by the Hungarian outlet Népszabadság (source in Hungarian), the programme may take in three cities and include cultural events alongside the political talks.

Security is a concern: in mid-November a drone attack hit the area around Mukachevo (Munkács in Hungarian), one of the region's main towns.

Citing the regional military administration (source in Ukrainian), the Hungarian-language news portal Kárpátalja.ma has warned residents to expect traffic restrictions in several places during the visit.

Magyar and Zelenskyy have already met at EU and NATO summits. However, Budapest had made a bilateral meeting conditional on Kyiv meeting its demands over the rights of Ukraine's Hungarian minority.

Magyar signalled that the meeting was imminent in a speech to the Hungarian parliament on Monday. In it, he accused the government of his predecessor, Viktor Orbán, of running a "hate-inciting" election campaign against Ukraine and its president. His government, he said, would stand up for the Hungarians of Zakarpattia and for the Ukrainian people under attack, even if Moscow objected.

Magyar said he would bring Hungary's message to the Hungarians of Zakarpattia. He said they had spent almost five years suffering, living in fear and freezing through the winters since Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

He stressed that Russia was the aggressor and that Ukraine and its people were the victims. He added that Hungary would continue to support Ukraine, though not with weapons or troops, but with humanitarian aid and diplomatic backing.

While Paris and London remain ‘firmly established favourites’ for train travellers, Rail Europe data shows that Ravenna, Bolzano, Linz and theme-park gateways are attracting ‘growing attention’.

The Italian city of Ravenna is among the European destinations seeing the fastest growth in searches by travel agents and tour operators, according to new data by Rail Europe.

The train booking platform’s “Track Record” report, which covers booking and search activity between 1 October 2025 and 31 October 2026, also points to growing interest in destinations from the Italian Alps to the station serving Disneyland Paris.

Paris, London and Italy’s major cities remain “firmly established favourites” for train travel, Rail Europe said. But the data suggests that the “next interesting client itinerary may begin somewhere less obvious” – from a city break in eastern Germany to a family trip to a theme park.

Ravenna tops the list for advance bookings

Known for its stunning mosaics, Ravenna is “attracting growing attention” and stood out in two parts of the report.

It was among the fastest-rising searches by travel professionals, while passengers who booked directly through Rail Europe reserved their journeys an average of 57 days before departure. That was the longest average booking lead time recorded in the report’s consumer analysis.

The two findings reflect separate groups, with one tracking where agents and tour operators searched and the other measuring how far ahead travellers booked.

Bolzano and the French Alps draw attention

Bolzano in South Tyrol also gained ground in searches by travel agents and tour operators following the 2026 Winter Olympic Games. Elsewhere in northern Italy, Bergamo drew growing interest from consumers.

Across the border in France, Chambéry and Grenoble were among the fastest-rising destinations for consumers on the platform.

Both cities are gateways to the French Alps, and travellers planning a rail trip that takes in both France and northern Italy can again use the Paris-Milan line, which reopened in 2025.

Theme parks and city breaks feature in searches

There is also a “different kind of destination emerging in the data”, Rail Europe said, with two train stations serving major European theme parks also seeing a rise in search interest among both consumers and travel professionals. Ringsheim is the railway gateway to Germany’s Europa-Park, while Marne-la-Vallée serves Disneyland Paris.

“Here, the railway station is closely tied to the experience the traveller wants to book,” Rail Europe said. “For travel professionals, knowing which stations are attracting interest can be as useful as knowing which cities are popular.”

Austria’s Linz and the German cities of Leipzig and Dresden were also among the fastest-rising searches overall. Rail Europe highlighted concert halls and Christmas markets among the attractions in these cities, offering ideas for trips built around a performance or a festive weekend.
